battle:乘丘之战.cmd: Prince Yan and Duke Zhuang of Lu vs. Nangong Changwan
battle:乘丘之战.mod: NW of Yanzhou, Shandong (one view: SW of Juye)
battle:乘丘之战.note: The allied Qi and Song armies encamped at Lang. Prince Yan of Lu covered his horses with tiger skins and struck the Song army first, Duke Zhuang of Lu followed, and they routed the Song army at Chengqiu; the Song general Nangong Changwan was captured.

battle:乾时之战.cmd: Duke Huan of Qi vs. Duke Zhuang of Lu
battle:乾时之战.mod: W of Linzi District, Zibo, Shandong (on the Shi River)
battle:乾时之战.note: Prince Xiaobai reached Qi first and became Duke Huan; Duke Zhuang of Lu, escorting Prince Jiu to contest the throne, was routed at Ganshi. Lu killed Prince Jiu and sent Guan Zhong to Qi as a prisoner, and Duke Huan made him chancellor.

battle:令狐之战.cmd: Zhao Dun vs. Duke Kang of Qin
battle:令狐之战.note: When Duke Xiang of Jin died, Zhao Dun at first sent to Qin for Prince Yong, and Duke Kang of Qin escorted him; but Zhao Dun then enthroned Duke Ling instead and turned on the Qin army at Linghu, and the Qin army went home defeated.

battle:伊洛之戎伐周.note: Prince Dai summoned the Rong of Yangju, Quangao and the Yi and Luo to attack the capital together; they entered Wangcheng and burned its east gate. Qin and Jin attacked the Rong to rescue Zhou, and Prince Dai fled to Qi.
battle:伊洛之戎伐周.old: The Rong of the Yi and Luo attack Zhou
battle:伊洛之戎伐周.sides: The Rong defeated Zhou (Qin and Jin attacked the Rong to rescue Zhou)

battle:伐山戎之役.cmd: Duke Huan of Qi and Guan Zhong
battle:伐山戎之役.note: The Mountain Rong were harassing Yan, and Duke Huan of Qi marched north against them, reaching Guzhu before turning back. Duke Zhuang of Yan escorted Duke Huan into Qi territory, and Duke Huan gave Yan the land as far as the Yan ruler had come. The idiom "an old horse knows the way" comes from this campaign.
battle:伐山戎之役.sides: Qi and Yan defeated the Mountain Rong

battle:伐皋落氏之役.mod: NE of Yuanqu, Shanxi (one view: Xiyang)
battle:伐皋落氏之役.note: Duke Xian of Jin sent Crown Prince Shensheng against the Gaoluo lineage of Dongshan. Shensheng set out wearing a two-coloured robe and a metal jue (slit ring) pendant, and came back after a great victory. From then on Li Ji's slanders grew more pressing.

battle:伐邽冀之戎.note: Duke Wu of Qin attacked the Rong of Gui and Ji and made their lands counties, the first counties set up by Qin; the next year he also made Du and Zheng counties and destroyed Lesser Guo.
battle:伐邽冀之戎.old: Campaign against the Rong of Gui and Ji

battle:假道灭虢.cmd: Duke Xian of Jin and Xun Xi vs. Chou, duke of Guo
battle:假道灭虢.note: Duke Xian of Jin gave the horses of Qu and the jade disc of Chuiji to borrow a road through Yu, and in 658 BC took Xiayang from Guo. In 655 BC he borrowed the road again; Gong Zhiqi's warning that "when the lips are gone the teeth are cold" went unheeded, and Jin destroyed Guo and, on its way home, Yu.
battle:假道灭虢.old: Borrowing a road to conquer Guo

battle:偪阳之役.mod: S of Yicheng District, Zaozhuang, Shandong
battle:偪阳之役.note: Jin gathered the lords to attack Biyang so as to enfeoff Xiang Xu of Song with it. The people of Biyang opened their gate to lure the attackers in; Shuliang He of Lu (Confucius's father) held up the portcullis with his hands so that the lords' soldiers could get out. Biyang was destroyed and given to Song.
battle:偪阳之役.sides: Jin and the feudal lords defeated Biyang

battle:吴入州来.cmd: Shoumeng, king of Wu, vs. Zizhong
battle:吴入州来.note: Wuchen, an exile from Chu, went to Wu as an envoy and taught it the use of chariots, archery and charioteering, and battle formations. Wu began to attack Chu, Chao and Xu and entered Zhoulai, and Zizhong of Chu "rushed off on campaign seven times in one year".

battle:吴灭徐.cmd: Helü vs. Zhangyu, viscount of Xu
battle:吴灭徐.note: The viscount of Xu sheltered Yanyu, a fugitive Wu prince. Helü dammed the mountain streams to flood Xu and destroyed it; the viscount of Xu cut off his hair and came out with his wife to meet the king of Wu, then fled to Chu. The same year Wu destroyed Zhongwu.

battle:城濮之战.cmd: Duke Wen of Jin and Xian Zhen vs. Cheng Dechen (Ziyu)
battle:城濮之战.mod: SW of Juancheng, Shandong (one view: between Fan County and Puyang, Henan)
battle:城濮之战.note: Duke Wen of Jin "withdrew three days' march" to repay a past kindness from Chu, luring the Chu army deep into the field. Xu Chen, his horses covered in tiger skins, first broke Chen and Cai (the Chu right); Xian Zhen struck the Chu left from the flank with the central army, and Ziyu withdrew and later killed himself. After the battle came the Covenant of Jiantu, and Duke Wen of Jin became hegemon.
battle:城濮之战.sides: Jin, Qin, Qi and Song defeated Chu, Chen and Cai

battle:大原之战.note: Xun Wu of Jin defeated Wuzhong and the various Di at Taiyuan. Because the Rong and Di were mostly foot soldiers and the ground was narrow and rugged, Wei Shu "broke up the chariots to form ranks", turning chariot troops into infantry formations; this was the first time infantry fought on its own.
battle:大原之战.sides: Jin defeated Wuzhong and the Di tribes

battle:大棘之战.mod: S of Sui County, Henan (one view: NW of Zhecheng)
battle:大棘之战.note: Zheng attacked Song on Chu's orders. Hua Yuan of Song slaughtered sheep to feed his men but left out his charioteer Yang Zhen, who drove the chariot into the Zheng army: "With the mutton the other day, you were in charge." Hua Yuan was captured and the Song army routed.

battle:夫椒之战.cmd: Fuchai and Wu Zixu vs. Goujian
battle:夫椒之战.mod: Xishan, Lake Tai, Wuzhong District, Suzhou, Jiangsu (one view: N of Shaoxing, Zhejiang)
battle:夫椒之战.note: Fuchai defeated Yue at Fujiao and went on into Yue. Goujian held out in the Kuaiji Mountains with five thousand armoured shield-bearers, sent Wen Zhong to sue for peace with Wu, and went to Wu to serve as its subject.

battle:宋灭曹.cmd: Duke Jing of Song vs. Yang, earl of Cao
battle:宋灭曹.note: Yang, earl of Cao, loved hunting and fowling; following Gongsun Qiang's plan, he broke with Jin and provoked Song. Duke Jing of Song attacked, Jin did not come to the rescue, and Song destroyed Cao, taking Yang, earl of Cao, and Gongsun Qiang back to Song and executing them.

battle:崤之战.cmd: Xian Zhen vs. Mengming Shi, Xiqi Shu and Baiyi Bing
battle:崤之战.mod: NW of Luoning – SE of Shanzhou District, Henan (between East and West Xiao)
battle:崤之战.note: Ignoring Jian Shu's warning, Duke Mu of Qin sent his army on a long-range surprise attack on Zheng; it turned back after meeting Xian Gao, who feasted the troops, and destroyed Hua. Duke Xiang of Jin went to war in blackened mourning clothes and, with the Jiang Rong, ambushed the Qin army at Xiao; it was wiped out and its three commanders captured.
battle:崤之战.sides: Jin and the Jiang Rong defeated Qin

battle:平阴之战.cmd: Xun Yan and Shi Gai vs. Duke Ling of Qi
battle:平阴之战.note: Jin led the armies of the lords against Qi, and Duke Ling of Qi "dug a moat at Fangmen and held it". The Jin forces set up decoy troops and dragged brushwood to raise dust; the Qi army fled by night, and the Jin army advanced to besiege Linzi and burned its outer suburbs on all four sides.
battle:平阴之战.sides: Jin, Lu, Song, Wey, Zheng, Cao, Ju, Zhu, Teng, Xue, Qi and Lesser Zhu defeated Qi

battle:彭衙之战.note: Mengming Shi led an army against Jin to avenge the Battle of Xiao; Xian Juju of Jin defeated him at Pengya, and the Jin mocked it as "the army come to give thanks for our kindness".

battle:晋灭潞氏.cmd: Xun Linfu vs. Feng Shu and Ying'er, viscount of Lu
battle:晋灭潞氏.note: Feng Shu, chief minister of the Lu lineage of the Red Di, seized power, killed the wife of the viscount of Lu (an elder sister of Duke Jing of Jin) and injured the viscount's eye. Xun Linfu of Jin defeated the Red Di at Quliang and destroyed the Lu lineage. The next year Jin also destroyed the Jia lineage and Liuxu.
battle:晋灭潞氏.old: Jin conquest of the Lu lineage

battle:晋灭陆浑.cmd: Xun Wu vs. the viscount of Luhun
battle:晋灭陆浑.note: On the pretext of a sacrifice to the Luo, Xun Wu led a Jin army across at Jijin Ford and made a surprise attack on Luhun. The viscount of Luhun fled to Chu and his people to Ganlu, and Jin took all their land.

battle:晋灭鼓.cmd: Xun Wu vs. Yuandi, viscount of Gu
battle:晋灭鼓.note: Xun Wu besieged Gu for three months. When the people of Gu offered to surrender, he refused because they still had strength left, and took the town only after their food ran out: "he conquered Gu and returned without putting a single man to death". In 520 BC Gu rebelled and Jin destroyed it again.

battle:朝歌之役.note: Taking advantage of the Luan lineage's revolt in Jin, Duke Zhuang of Qi attacked Jin and took Zhaoge; he split his forces to go through Mengmen and up the Taihang Mountains, raised a mound at the Shao River and returned. It was the deepest a Qi army went into Jin in the Spring and Autumn period.
battle:朝歌之役.sides: Qi defeated Jin (Qi took Zhaoge and withdrew)

battle:朱方之役.cmd: King Ling of Chu vs. Qing Feng
battle:朱方之役.note: King Ling of Chu gathered the lords at Shen and led Cai, Chen, Xu and others against Wu. He besieged Zhufang, seized Qing Feng, an exile from Qi, and wiped out his clan. Wu promptly struck back at the Chu towns of Ji, Li and Ma in revenge.

battle:柏举之战.cmd: Helü, Sun Wu, Wu Zixu and Fugai vs. Nang Wa (Zichang)
battle:柏举之战.note: Wu left its boats at Huairui and struck deep into Chu through three passes, Dasui, Zhiyuan and Ming'e Pass. At Baiju the Chu army collapsed; the Wu army won five battles to reach Ying, King Zhao of Chu fled, and Wu Zixu flogged the corpse of King Ping.
battle:柏举之战.sides: Wu, Cai and Tang defeated Chu

battle:楚伐罗之战.mod: W of Yicheng, Hubei (on the Yan River)
battle:楚伐罗之战.note: Qu Xia attacked Luo but, underrating the enemy, took no precautions; Luo and the Lu Rong attacked from both sides and routed the Chu army, and Qu Xia hanged himself at Huanggu.
battle:楚伐罗之战.sides: Luo and the Lu Rong defeated Chu

battle:楚围宋.cmd: King Zhuang of Chu vs. Hua Yuan
battle:楚围宋.note: Song killed the Chu envoy Shen Zhou as he passed through, and King Zhuang of Chu besieged Song for nine months; in the city people "exchanged children to eat and split bones for firewood". Hua Yuan slipped into the Chu camp by night to persuade Zifan, and the two states made a covenant and ended the war.
battle:楚围宋.sides: Chu defeated Song (Song made peace with Chu)

battle:楚灭蔡.cmd: Prince Qiji vs. Crown Prince You of Cai
battle:楚灭蔡.note: King Ling of Chu lured Marquis Ling of Cai to Shen and killed him, then sent Prince Qiji to besiege and destroy Cai. He made Qiji duke of Cai and sacrificed the crown prince of Cai at Mount Gang.

battle:檇李之战.note: Helü attacked Yue during the mourning for Yunchang, king of Yue. Goujian sent three ranks of convicts up to the Wu lines to cut their own throats; while the Wu army stared in shock, the Yue army attacked, and Helü was wounded in the foot and died. Fuchai swore to avenge his father.

battle:汾隰之战.cmd: Duke Wu of Quwo and Han Wan vs. Marquis Ai of Jin
battle:汾隰之战.mod: Fen River lowlands between Yicheng and Quwo, Shanxi
battle:汾隰之战.note: Duke Wu of Quwo attacked Yi and pursued Marquis Ai of Jin at Fenxi; the marquis's outer horse caught on a tree and his chariot stopped, and that night he was captured (later killed by Han Wan). Quwo was now set to supplant Yi.

battle:河曲之战.cmd: Zhao Dun vs. Duke Kang of Qin
battle:河曲之战.mod: SW of Yongji, Shanxi (at the bend of the Yellow River)
battle:河曲之战.note: Duke Kang of Qin attacked Jin and took Jima, and Zhao Dun met him at Hequ. Yu Pian urged deepening the ramparts and waiting, but Zhao Chuan went out on his own to seek battle; the two armies clashed and both drew back, and the Qin army slipped away by night.
battle:河曲之战.sides: Qin and Jin in stalemate (the Qin army fled by night)

battle:泓上之役.cmd: Chou Wuyu and Ou Yang vs. Crown Prince You
battle:泓上之役.note: Fuchai had gone north to meet the lords at Huangchi, taking all his best troops. Goujian seized the chance to attack Wu, defeated the Wu army, captured Crown Prince You and entered the Wu capital. Fuchai kept the news secret and hurried home to sue for peace.

battle:泓之战.cmd: Cheng Dechen vs. Duke Xiang of Song
battle:泓之战.note: Duke Xiang of Song held that one should "not drum the attack before the enemy is in formation" and "not take grey-haired men captive"; he waited until the Chu army had crossed the Hong River and drawn up its lines before giving battle, and was routed. Wounded in the thigh, he died the next year. His dream of hegemony was shattered.

battle:津之战.note: The Ba rebelled against Chu, attacked Nachu and then invaded Chu, and King Wen of Chu was routed at Jin. Yu Quan refused to let the king back in, so King Wen turned to attack Huang, and he died at Jiao on the way home.

battle:湛阪之战.cmd: Xun Yan and Luan Yan vs. Prince Ge
battle:湛阪之战.note: Duke Ping of Jin had just come to the throne. The Jin army attacked Xu and then Chu, defeated the Chu army at Zhanban, and raided the land beyond Fangcheng before turning back.

battle:灭庸之役.note: Chu was in the grip of a great famine when Yong led the Man tribes in revolt. King Zhuang of Chu made the enemy overconfident by "fleeing in all seven encounters", then joined with Qin and Ba to destroy Yong. This was the start of the rise of King Zhuang of Chu, who "startled the world with a single cry".
battle:灭庸之役.sides: Chu, Qin and Ba defeated Yong

battle:狄伐邢.note: The Di attacked Xing. Guan Zhong urged Duke Huan of Qi: "The Rong and Di are jackals and wolves; they can never be satisfied." Qi sent troops to rescue Xing, and in 659 BC the lords moved Xing to Yiyi.

battle:王官之役.cmd: Duke Mu of Qin and Mengming Shi
battle:王官之役.note: Duke Mu of Qin led the campaign himself. He crossed the He and burned his boats, and took Wangguan and Jiao from Jin; Jin did not come out to fight. He then crossed the He at Maojin Ford, raised a burial mound over the dead at Xiao and returned.

battle:秦伐西戎.cmd: Duke Mu of Qin and You Yu
battle:秦伐西戎.note: Duke Mu of Qin followed You Yu's plans to attack the Rong king, "adding twelve states and opening up a thousand li of land, and so became hegemon of the Western Rong". King Xiang of Zhou sent Guo, duke of Shao, to congratulate him with a gift of gongs and drums.

battle:秦文公伐戎.note: Duke Wen of Qin sent troops against the Rong, who fled in defeat. He then took in the remaining Zhou people and held their land as far as Mount Qi, presenting the land east of Mount Qi to Zhou. From then on Qin held the western part of Guanzhong.
battle:秦文公伐戎.old: Duke Wen of Qin attacks the Rong

battle:笠泽之战.mod: S of Suzhou, Jiangsu (around the Wusong River)
battle:笠泽之战.note: The Wu and Yue armies drew up facing each other across Li Marsh. At night Goujian had his left and right armies beat their drums and feign crossings, drawing off the Wu forces, while his central army slipped across and struck straight at the Wu centre; the Wu army was routed. Afterwards Yue besieged Wu for three years.

battle:箕之战.cmd: Xian Zhen and Xi Que vs. the viscount of the White Di
battle:箕之战.mod: E of Taigu, Shanxi (one view: NE of Pu County)
battle:箕之战.note: The Di attacked Jin as far as Ji. Duke Xiang of Jin defeated them, and Xi Que captured the viscount of the White Di. Xian Zhen, considering that he had been disrespectful to his ruler, took off his helmet, charged into the Di army and was killed.

battle:繻葛之战.cmd: Duke Zhuang of Zheng and Zhu Dan vs. King Huan of Zhou
battle:繻葛之战.note: King Huan of Zhou led Chen, Cai and Wey against Zheng. Duke Zhuang of Zheng, using the "fish-scale formation", first routed Chen, Cai and Wey and then closed on the royal army from both sides; Zhu Dan shot the king in the shoulder. The prestige of the Zhou Son of Heaven was shattered.
battle:繻葛之战.sides: Zheng defeated Zhou, Chen, Cai and Wey

battle:舒鸠之役.note: Shujiu broke with Chu and went over to Wu. Qu Jian, chief minister of Chu, attacked it; Wu came to Shujiu's rescue and was beaten by the Chu army, and Chu then destroyed Shujiu. All the lands of the Qunshu passed to Chu.

battle:艾陵之战.mod: NE of Laiwu District, Jinan, Shandong (one view: SE of Tai'an)
battle:艾陵之战.note: Fuchai, king of Wu, marched north against Qi, joined forces with Lu and crushed the Qi army at Ailing, capturing and killing the Qi general Guo Shu and taking eight hundred leather-armoured chariots and the heads of three thousand armoured men. Wu's power was at its height.

battle:荧泽之战.mod: around Xun County and Qi County (Hebi), Henan (location disputed; one view: the same as the Xing Marsh)
battle:荧泽之战.note: Duke Yi of Wey loved cranes, and some of his cranes even rode in grandees' carriages, so his people would not fight for him. The Di routed the Wey army at Ying Marsh and killed Duke Yi, and the survivors of Wey crossed the Yellow River to the east.

battle:莘之战.cmd: King Wen of Chu vs. Marquis Ai of Cai
battle:莘之战.note: The marquis of Xi, resenting Marquis Ai of Cai's discourtesy to Xi Gui, drew Chu into attacking Cai; Chu defeated the Cai army at Shen and captured Marquis Ai of Cai. In 680 BC Chu went on to destroy Xi.

battle:蒲骚之战.cmd: Dou Lian and Qu Xia vs. Yun
battle:蒲骚之战.note: The men of Yun encamped at Pusao, planning to attack Chu together with Sui, Jiao, Zhou and Liao; Dou Lian made a night attack on the Yun army and defeated it, and Chu went on to make a covenant with Er and Zhen.

battle:辅氏之战.note: Duke Huan of Qin attacked Jin; Wei Ke defeated Qin at Fushi and captured the Qin strongman Du Hui. By tradition Wei Ke had married off his father's concubine instead of having her buried with his father, and her father, an old man, repaid him by knotting grass to trip Du Hui.

battle:速杞之战.cmd: King Wu of Chu vs. the marquis of Sui
battle:速杞之战.mod: between Suizhou and Guangshui, Hubei (one view)
battle:速杞之战.note: King Wu of Chu gathered the lords at Shenlu; when Sui failed to come, Chu attacked it and defeated the Sui army at Suqi, and Sui sued for peace. The same year King Wu of Chu proclaimed himself king.

battle:邲之战.cmd: King Zhuang of Chu and Sunshu Ao vs. Xun Linfu and Xian Hu
battle:邲之战.mod: N of Zhengzhou, Henan (NE of Xingyang)
battle:邲之战.note: Chu besieged Zheng, and the earl of Zheng surrendered bare-chested, leading a sheep. Jin came too late to relieve Zheng; Xian Hu crossed the He without orders, and the Jin army was routed and fought over the boats to recross the river until "the fingers in the boats could be scooped up by the handful". With this King Zhuang of Chu became hegemon.

battle:鄢陵之战.cmd: Luan Shu and Xi Zhi vs. King Gong of Chu and Zifan
battle:鄢陵之战.note: Jin and Chu fought over Zheng and met at Yanling. Lü Qi shot King Gong of Chu in the eye, and the Chu army slipped away by night; Zifan, who had failed in his duty through drunkenness, was forced to kill himself. After this Chu's power declined.

battle:钟离之役.note: Women of Beiliang, a Wu border town, and of Zhongli, a Chu border town, quarrelled over mulberry trees; the two towns attacked each other, and then the two states went to war. Prince Guang attacked Chu, destroyed Chao and Zhongli and returned.

battle:铁之战.cmd: Zhao Yang vs. Han Da and Si Hong
battle:铁之战.note: During the revolt of the Fan and Zhonghang lineages in Jin, Qi sent grain to the Fan lineage under a Zheng escort. Zhao Yang swore to his army: "Whoever defeats the enemy shall, if a senior grandee, receive a county, and if a junior grandee, a commandery." He defeated the Zheng army at Tie and seized a thousand cartloads of grain.
battle:铁之战.sides: The Zhao lineage of Jin defeated Zheng and the Fan lineage

battle:长勺之战.cmd: Cao Gui and Duke Zhuang of Lu vs. Duke Huan of Qi
battle:长勺之战.mod: NE of Laiwu District, Jinan, Shandong (one view: N of Qufu)
battle:长勺之战.note: Qi attacked Lu. Cao Gui asked to fight; he waited until Qi had sounded its drums three times before attacking, and the Qi army was routed. "With the first drum the spirit is roused, with the second it flags, with the third it is spent."

battle:长岸之战.mod: SW of Dangtu, Anhui (between the East and West Liang Mountains)
battle:长岸之战.note: The Wu and Chu fleets fought at Chang'an. Chu won and captured the Wu king's ship, the Yuhuang; but Prince Guang sent men by night to hide beside the ship and throw the Chu forces into confusion with false shouts, and recaptured the Yuhuang and brought it home.
battle:长岸之战.sides: Chu defeated Wu (Wu recaptured the Yuhuang)

battle:雍澨之战.cmd: Zipu, Zihu and Zixi vs. Fugai
battle:雍澨之战.note: Shen Baoxu wept at the Qin court for seven days, and Duke Ai of Qin sent five hundred chariots to save Chu. The allied Qin and Chu armies defeated Wu at Yi and Yongshi; Wu was also shaken by Fugai's bid to make himself king, so Helü took his army home, and King Zhao of Chu recovered his state.

battle:鞌之战.cmd: Xi Ke vs. Duke Qing of Qi
battle:鞌之战.mod: N of Licheng District, Jinan, Shandong (at the foot of Mount Huafuzhu)
battle:鞌之战.note: Xi Ke, humiliated on a mission to Qi, swore revenge. At the Battle of An the Qi army was routed; Pang Choufu changed places with Duke Qing, who escaped. Qi returned the land it had seized from Lu and Wey and made a covenant.
battle:鞌之战.sides: Jin, Lu, Wey and Cao defeated Qi

battle:韩原之战.cmd: Duke Mu of Qin vs. Duke Hui of Jin
battle:韩原之战.mod: between Hejin and Wanrong, Shanxi (one view: SW of Hancheng, Shaanxi)
battle:韩原之战.note: Duke Hui of Jin broke his promise to cede the land of Hexi and also refused to sell grain to Qin. Duke Mu of Qin attacked Jin; Duke Hui's chariot stuck in the mud and he was captured. Mu Ji pleaded for him, Duke Hui was allowed home, and Jin ceded the land of Hexi.

battle:骊山之役.cmd: The marquis of Shen vs. King You of Zhou
battle:骊山之役.mod: foot of Mount Li, Lintong District, Xi'an, Shaanxi
battle:骊山之役.note: King You deposed Queen Shen and Crown Prince Yijiu; the marquis of Shen joined with Zeng and the Quanrong to attack Zongzhou and killed King You at the foot of Mount Li, and the Western Zhou fell. The next year King Ping moved east to Luoyi.
battle:骊山之役.sides: Shen, Zeng and the Quanrong defeated Zhou

battle:鸠兹之战.note: Zizhong of Chu attacked Wu, took Jiuzi and advanced to Mount Heng; the Wu forces intercepted the Chu army and captured the Chu general Deng Liao. Zizhong returned home and died of a heart ailment. The struggle between Wu and Chu intensified from then on.

battle:鸡父之战.note: Wu attacked Zhoulai, and the Chu chief minister Yang Gai fell ill and died with the army. Wu sent three thousand convicts to strike first at the forces of Hu, Shen and Chen and routed them; the rulers of Hu and Shen were killed. Wu then took Zhoulai.
battle:鸡父之战.sides: Wu defeated Chu, Dun, Hu, Shen, Cai, Chen and Xu

battle:麻隧之战.cmd: Luan Shu vs. Duke Huan of Qin
battle:麻隧之战.note: Duke Li of Jin sent Lü Xiang to break off relations with Qin and led the armies of the lords against it, defeating Qin at Masui; they crossed the Jing River and reached Houli before turning back. For a long time afterwards Qin was too weak to push east.
battle:麻隧之战.sides: Jin, Lu, Qi, Song, Wey, Zheng, Cao, Zhu and Teng defeated Qin

battle:齐灭莱.cmd: Yan Ruo vs. Duke Gong of Lai
battle:齐灭莱.mod: S of Jimo, Shandong (Tang; one view: Guicheng, Longkou)
battle:齐灭莱.note: Duke Ling of Qi had Yan Ruo fortify Dongyang to put pressure on Lai, then besieged Tang and destroyed Lai, moving Duke Gong of Lai to Ni. Qi's territory now reached the sea in the east and took in all of Jiaodong.

capital:上庸.note: Capital of the state of Yong, which had joined King Wu in his campaign against King Zhou of Shang. In 611 BC the people of Yong led the Man tribes, and the people of Jun the Hundred Pu, in revolt against Chu, and Chu, allied with Qin and Ba, destroyed Yong.

capital:上蔡.note: Capital of Cai, enfeoffed to Shu Du, younger brother of King Wu. Chu destroyed Cai in 531 BC; in 529 BC King Ping of Chu restored Cai, which moved to Xincai.

capital:上阳.note: Capital of West Guo after it moved east (North Guo), facing Xiayang on the north bank of the He. The Cemetery of the State of Guo at Sanmenxia has yielded the tombs of Guo Ji and Guo Zhong.

capital:下蔡.note: Originally Zhoulai. In 493 BC Marquis Zhao of Cai, fearing Chu, moved to Zhoulai, then under Wu's control, and it was called Xiacai. King Hui of Chu destroyed Cai in 447 BC.

capital:东虢.note: Descendants of Guo Shu, younger brother of King Wen of Zhou, holding the stronghold of Zhi (Hulao). Destroyed by Duke Wu of Zheng in 767 BC.

capital:中人.note: A Xianyu town: in 529 BC Xun Wu of Jin invaded Xianyu "as far as Zhongren"; one view holds it was an early capital of Xianyu (Zhongshan). When Duke Wu of Zhongshan first came to power (414 BC) he lived at Gu.

capital:临淄.note: Capital of Qi (Yingqiu). Duke Huan of Qi employed Guan Zhong and "nine times assembled the lords and set the whole realm aright"; Linzi was the greatest city of the east in the Spring and Autumn.

capital:丹阳.mod: Xichuan, Henan (confluence of the Dan and Xi rivers; location disputed)
capital:丹阳.note: Early capital of Chu, where Xiong Yi lived. Its location is much debated: one view puts it where the Dan and Xi rivers meet, another at Zigui or Zhijiang in Hubei.

capital:义渠.note: Capital of the Yiqu Rong. Yiqu built inner and outer walls to defend itself; in the Spring and Autumn it alternately fought and made peace with Qin, and was Qin's formidable enemy in the northwest.

capital:会稽.note: In 490 BC Goujian returned from Wu, and Fan Li built a city north of the Kuaiji Mountains; "sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall" and "ten years to multiply and gather, ten years to teach and train" both took place here.

capital:六.note: The Yan-surnamed state of Lu, descended from Gaoyao. Destroyed by Cheng Daxin of Chu in 622 BC.

capital:古魏城.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Wei, enfeoffed under the Western Zhou. In 661 BC Duke Xian of Jin destroyed Wei and gave it to Bi Wan: the origin of the Warring States Wei lineage.

capital:叶.note: In 576 BC Chu moved Xu to She. In 533 BC it was moved for a time to Yi (Chengfu), returned to She in 529 BC, and in 524 BC was moved again, to Baiyu.

capital:吴.note: In 514 BC Helü had Wu Zixu build the "Great City of Helü" (one view: the Mudu ancient city); Wu's hegemony centred here. Yue destroyed Wu in 473 BC.

capital:唐.mod: Tangxian Town, NW of Suizhou, Hubei
capital:唐.note: The Qi-surnamed state of Tang. Duke Cheng of Tang was detained by Zichang, the Chu chief minister, over his Sushuang horses; in 506 BC he joined Wu in attacking Chu, and in 505 BC Chu destroyed Tang.

capital:商丘.note: Capital of Song, enfeoffed to Weizi Qi, home of the descendants of the Shang; Duke Xiang of Song's bid for hegemony and Xiang Xu's effort to end war both centred here.

capital:埤中.note: An early capital of Yue; its location is unknown, one view placing it in modern Zhuji.

capital:大荔王城.note: The Dali Rong built dozens of walled towns, styled themselves king and had their capital at Wangcheng. In 461 BC Duke Ligong of Qin attacked Dali with twenty thousand troops and took its Wangcheng.

capital:夷仪.mod: SW of Liaocheng, Shandong (one view: W of Xingtai, Hebei)
capital:夷仪.note: In 659 BC the lords walled Yiyi and moved Xing there: "Xing moved as if coming home". In 635 BC Duke Wen of Wey destroyed Xing.

capital:宛丘.note: Capital of Chen, enfeoffed to Gui Man, descendant of Shun: "boom goes the drum below Wanqiu" (Odes, "Airs of Chen"). Destroyed by King Hui of Chu in 478 BC.

capital:容城.mod: SE of Lushan, Henan (one view: W of Ye County)
capital:容城.note: Xu moved to Rongcheng in 506 BC, after which it dwindled; early in the Warring States it was destroyed by Chu (one view: by Wei), date unknown.

capital:少梁.note: The Ying-surnamed state of Liang, of the same ancestry as Qin. The earl of Liang was fond of building works until his worn-out people deserted; in 641 BC Qin destroyed Liang, and its land was later called Shaoliang.

capital:巢.note: The state of Chao, a key place between the Yangtze and the Huai contested by Wu and Chu. In 548 BC Zhufan, king of Wu, attacked the gate of Chao and died of an arrow wound; Wu destroyed Chao in 518 BC.

capital:平阳.mod: Yangping Town, Chencang District, Baoji, Shaanxi
capital:平阳.note: In the 2nd year of Duke Ning of Qin (714 BC) the capital moved to Pingyang; Duke Wu of Qin's attack on the Rong of Gui and Ji, and the first counties set up there, also fall in this period.

capital:徐.note: The Ying-surnamed state of Xu, which rivalled Zhou in the Western Zhou (King Yan of Xu). In the Spring and Autumn it was caught between Qi, Chu and Wu; Wu destroyed Xu in 512 BC.

capital:息.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Xi. In 684 BC the marquis of Xi drew Chu into attacking Cai; in 680 BC King Wen of Chu destroyed Xi and took Xi Gui as his consort.

capital:成周.mod: E of Luoyang, Henan (around the Han–Wei Luoyang ruins)
capital:成周.note: One of the eastern capitals built by the Duke of Zhou. After the rebellion of Prince Zhao, King Jing lived here; in 510 BC Jin led the lords in walling Chengzhou, and thereafter the Zhou kings mostly resided at Chengzhou.

capital:新田.note: In 585 BC Duke Jing of Jin moved the capital to Xintian, which was called New Jiang. The Jin city site at Houma is vast, and the Houma covenant texts were found here.

capital:新蔡.note: In 529 BC King Ping of Chu restored Cai, and Marquis Ping of Cai moved the capital here.

capital:新郑.note: Built by Duke Wu of Zheng after he destroyed Kuai and East Guo; Zheng's capital for four hundred years. Zheng lay at the centre of the realm, and while Jin and Chu contended for hegemony it waited "with sacrificial animals, jade and silk at both borders".

capital:曲沃.note: The town enfeoffed to Huan Shu: "Quwo is larger than Yi". After destroying Yi and taking over Jin in 678 BC, Duke Wu still lived here, until Duke Xian moved to Jiang in 669 BC.

capital:曲阜.note: Capital of Lu, enfeoffed to Boqin, son of the Duke of Zhou: "the rites of Zhou are all in Lu". The Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals) is the record kept by the Lu court historians.

capital:曹邑.note: After the Di destroyed Wey, Duke Huan of Song received the seven hundred and thirty survivors of Wey, added people from Gong and Teng to make five thousand, and set up Duke Dai, who lodged at Cao.

capital:朝歌.note: Originally a late Shang capital; the Duke of Zhou enfeoffed Kang Shu here to found Wey. In 660 BC the Di crushed Wey, Duke Yi died, and the survivors crossed the Yellow River to the east.

capital:杞城.note: Capital of Qi in the early Spring and Autumn; its location is disputed. Bronzes of the earls of Qi have been found at Xintai, and one view places it there. In 646 BC, as the Huai Yi harried Qi, the lords moved it to Yuanling.

capital:梅里.note: By tradition where Taibo lived after fleeing to Wu. The location of the Wu capital before Shoumeng is uncertain; one view puts it at Meili.

capital:楚丘.note: In 658 BC Duke Huan of Qi led the lords in walling Chuqiu and re-established Wey there: "Wey forgot it had been lost". Duke Wen of Wey revived the state here.

capital:江.note: The Ying-surnamed state of Jiang. When Chu destroyed Jiang in 623 BC, Duke Mu of Qin, for its sake, wore plain clothes, moved out of his chambers and gave up his full meals.

capital:江州.note: Capital of Ba. In the Spring and Autumn the Ba people had dealings with Chu and Deng to the north and once helped Chu destroy Yong; the Ba capital moved several times, and this was a later one.

capital:汧.note: In the 2nd year of Duke Xiang of Qin (776 BC) the capital moved to Qian, and the Qin people stepped out of Longyou onto the western edge of Guanzhong.

capital:汧渭之会.mod: Chencang District, Baoji, Shaanxi (where the Qian River joins the Wei)
capital:汧渭之会.note: In 762 BC Duke Wen of Qin, hunting eastward, reached the confluence of the Qian and Wei, divined there and built a town; from here Qin pushed east to recover the land west of Mount Qi.
capital:汧渭之会.old: Confluence of the Qian and Wei

capital:沈.mod: N of Pingyu, Henan (Shen state ruins)
capital:沈.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Shen. When Shen stayed away from the Assembly at Shaoling in 506 BC, Cai destroyed it on Jin's orders.

capital:淳于.note: Originally the capital of the state of Zhou. In 544 BC Duke Ping of Jin assembled the lords to build walls for Qi, and Qi moved to Chunyu; in 445 BC King Hui of Chu destroyed Qi.

capital:滑.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Hua, with its capital at Fei. In 627 BC the Qin army, having failed in its surprise attack on Zheng, destroyed Hua and turned back, and on the way home was ambushed by Jin at Xiao.

capital:滕.mod: SW of Tengzhou, Shandong (Teng state ruins)
capital:滕.note: Capital of Teng, enfeoffed to Cuo Shu Xiu, son of King Wen of Zhou. Small as it was, Teng took its place at covenants, and disputed precedence with Xue at the court of Lu.

capital:潞.mod: Gucheng Village, NE of Lucheng, Shanxi
capital:潞.note: Capital of the Lu lineage of the Red Di. In 594 BC Xun Linfu of Jin destroyed the Lu lineage and brought back Ying'er, viscount of Lu, as a captive.

capital:濮阳.note: Diqiu, capital of Wey. Duke Cheng of Wey moved the capital here in 629 BC to escape the Di, and Diqiu remained the Wey capital for nearly four hundred years.

capital:王城.note: The royal city of Eastern Zhou (Luoyi), where King Ping lived after moving east. In 516 BC King Jing, avoiding Prince Zhao, entered Chengzhou; after that Wangcheng gradually became the residence of the lord of West Zhou.

capital:申.note: The Jiang-surnamed state of Shen (Southern Shen); King Xuan of Zhou enfeoffed the earl of Shen at Xie. Around 688 BC King Wen of Chu destroyed Shen and made it Shen County, a key base for Chu's advance north.

capital:白羽.note: That is, the town of Xi. In 524 BC Chu moved Xu to Baiyu.

capital:纪.note: The Jiang-surnamed state of Ji, a hereditary enemy of Qi. In 693 BC Qi relocated the three Ji towns of Ping, Zi and Wu; in 690 BC the marquis of Ji "left his state for good".

capital:绎.mod: SE of Zoucheng, Shandong (Zhu state ruins)
capital:绎.note: In 614 BC Duke Wen of Zhu divined about moving to Yi: "if it benefits the people, it benefits me"; and so he moved. In the Warring States it was called Zou, and it was destroyed by Chu in c. the mid-3rd century BC (date uncertain).

capital:绛.mod: SE of Yicheng, Shanxi (Old Jiang; location disputed)
capital:绛.note: In 669 BC Duke Xian of Jin walled Ju, named it Jiang and made it his capital, known to history as Old Jiang. Under Duke Xian, Duke Wen and Duke Xiang, Jin rose from here to hegemony.

capital:缘陵.note: In 646 BC Duke Huan of Qi assembled the lords to wall Yuanling and moved the state of Qi there, away from the Huai Yi.

capital:翼.mod: SE of Yicheng, Shanxi (one view: Tianma–Qucun site)
capital:翼.note: Early capital of Jin. In 745 BC Marquis Zhao enfeoffed his uncle Huan Shu at Quwo, after which Quwo and Yi fought each other for more than sixty years.

capital:耿.note: A small Ji-surnamed state. In 661 BC Duke Xian of Jin destroyed Geng and gave it to Zhao Su: the first fief of the Zhao lineage in Jin.

capital:肥.note: Capital of the White Di state of Fei. In 530 BC Xun Wu of Jin borrowed a road through Xianyu, entered Xiyang, destroyed Fei and brought back Miangao, viscount of Fei.

capital:胡.note: The Gui-surnamed state of Hu (one view: Ji surname). The ruler of Hu was killed by Wu at the Battle of Jifu in 519 BC; Chu destroyed Hu in 495 BC.

capital:舒.mod: SW of Lujiang, Anhui (one view: Shucheng)
capital:舒.note: One of the Qunshu, of the Yan surname. The Qunshu included Shu, Shuliao, Shuyong, Shujiu and others; Chu destroyed Shuliao in 601 BC and Shujiu in 548 BC, and all the Qunshu passed to Chu.

capital:芮.mod: S of Chaoyi Town, Dali, Shaanxi
capital:芮.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Rui, destroyed by Duke Mu of Qin in 640 BC. The great Rui tombs at Liangdai Village in Hancheng may mark Rui's early capital.

capital:莒.note: Capital of the Ji-surnamed state of Ju, a great power in the east: When Duke Huan of Qi fled abroad he took refuge in Ju: "do not forget the time in Ju". Chu destroyed Ju in 431 BC.

capital:莱.mod: Guicheng, SE of Longkou, Shandong (one view: SE of Changle)
capital:莱.note: The Jiang-surnamed state of Lai, a great power of the Eastern Yi that once contended with Qi for Yingqiu. In 567 BC Duke Ling of Qi destroyed Lai and moved Duke Gong of Lai to Ni.

capital:蓟.note: Capital of Yan. In the Spring and Autumn Yan lay remote in the north and was harried by the Mountain Rong; only Duke Huan of Qi's northern campaign of 663 BC brought it security.

capital:蓼.note: Descendants of Gaoyao and Tingjian. When Chu destroyed Liao in 622 BC, Zang Wenzhong lamented: "Gaoyao and Tingjian, so suddenly left without sacrifice!"

capital:薛.note: The Ren-surnamed state of Xue, descended from Xi Zhong. In the Warring States it was annexed by Qi (date unknown), and in 321 BC Qi enfeoffed Tian Ying there.

capital:虞.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Yu, descended from Taibo and Yuzhong. The duke of Yu, coveting Jin's jade disc and horses, let Jin borrow a road to attack Guo ("when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold"), and in 655 BC Yu fell along with Guo.

capital:西垂.mod: NE of Li County, Gansu (around Dabaozishan)
capital:西垂.note: Xiquanqiu, home of the Qin ancestors for generations. The great tombs of the Qin dukes and the Qin ducal bronzes found at Dabaozishan in Li County may mark the burial ground of Duke Xiang and Duke Wen.

capital:西郑.note: Where Duke Huan of Zheng was first enfeoffed. In 774 BC Duke Huan lodged his household between Guo and Kuai; his son Duke Wu followed King Ping east and built a new capital, Xinzheng.

capital:许.note: The Jiang-surnamed state of Xu, descended from the Four Mountains (Siyue). Duke Zhuang of Zheng entered Xu in 712 BC; in 576 BC Duke Ling of Xu, fearing Zheng, asked to be moved into Chu.

capital:谭.mod: W of Zhangqiu District, Jinan, Shandong (around Chengziya)
capital:谭.note: The Zi-surnamed state of Tan. When Duke Huan of Qi passed through Tan in exile, Tan showed him no courtesy; in 684 BC Qi destroyed Tan, and the viscount of Tan fled to Ju.

capital:遂.note: The Gui-surnamed state of Sui, descended from Shun. When the men of Sui failed to attend the Assembly at Beixing in 681 BC, Qi destroyed Sui and garrisoned it; in 677 BC the people of Sui killed the whole Qi garrison.

capital:邓.mod: N of Fancheng District, Xiangyang, Hubei (Dengcheng)
capital:邓.note: The Man-surnamed state of Deng. When King Wen of Chu passed through Deng on his way to attack Shen, Marquis Qi of Deng rejected the advice of the "three nephews" to kill him; in 678 BC Chu destroyed Deng.

capital:邢.note: Fief of a son of the Duke of Zhou. The Di attacked Xing in 661 BC; in 659 BC Qi, Song and Cao came to its rescue and moved Xing to Yiyi.

capital:邾.note: Early capital of Zhu; its location is unknown, one view placing it SE of modern Qufu. In 614 BC Duke Wen of Zhu moved to Yi.

capital:郐.note: The Yun-surnamed state of Kuai, between the Zhen and Wei rivers. Destroyed by Duke Wu of Zheng in 769 BC, after which the people of Zheng settled its land.

capital:郢.note: King Wen of Chu first made Ying his capital in 689 BC (whether the Spring and Autumn Ying was at Jinancheng is disputed). In 506 BC the Wu army entered Ying and King Zhao of Chu fled.

capital:郫.note: By tradition Duyu, styled Emperor Wang, had his capital at Pi; after the Kaiming lineage replaced Duyu, the ninth Kaiming ruler moved the seat to Chengdu (date unknown). The Jinsha site in Chengdu also belongs to this period.

capital:郯.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Tan, descended from Shaohao. In 525 BC the viscount of Tan paid court to Lu, and Confucius went to him to learn about the ancient offices: "when the Son of Heaven has lost his offices, learning survives among the four Yi".

capital:鄀.note: In 504 BC Wu defeated Chu again, and King Zhao of Chu moved the capital to Ruo and "reorganised his government". When the capital returned to Ying after King Zhao is not recorded; the map takes King Zhao's death as the cut-off.

capital:鄫.mod: NW of Lanling, Shandong (one view: E of Zaozhuang)
capital:鄫.note: The Si-surnamed state of Zeng, descended from Shaokang of Xia. Destroyed by Ju in 567 BC.

capital:钟离.note: The Ying-surnamed state of Zhongli (the tomb of Bai, lord of Zhongli, is at Shuangdun in Fengyang). Lying between Wu and Chu, it was destroyed by Wu in 518 BC.

capital:镐京.note: Capital of Western Zhou (Zongzhou). In 771 BC the marquis of Shen, allied with Zeng and the Quanrong, sacked Haojing; King You died at the foot of Mount Li, and the next year King Ping moved east.

capital:陆浑.note: In 638 BC Qin and Jin moved the Luhun Rong to Yichuan, and they settled here; in 525 BC Xun Wu of Jin destroyed Luhun, and the viscount of Luhun fled to Chu.

capital:陶丘.mod: NW of Dingtao District, Heze, Shandong
capital:陶丘.note: Capital of Cao, enfeoffed to Cao Shu Zhenduo, on the Ji River. Song destroyed Cao in 487 BC, and the place later became Tao, "the centre of the realm".

capital:随.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Sui (that is, Zeng), the great power east of the Han. In 506 BC King Zhao of Chu fled to Sui, and the people of Sui refused Wu's demand to hand him over. Absorbed into Chu in the early Warring States; date unknown.

capital:雍.note: Duke De of Qin first lived at Yong in his 1st year (677 BC); it was Qin's capital for nearly three hundred years. Site of Great Tomb No. 1 of the Qin dukes; it was also Duke Mu's base when he became hegemon of the Western Rong.

capital:雍丘.note: Where the state of Qi was first enfeoffed, to Duke Donglou, a descendant of Yu of Xia. Qi had moved east to Shandong before the late Western Zhou; the date is unknown.

capital:霍.note: Fief of Huo Shu Chu, son of King Wen of Zhou. Destroyed by Duke Xian of Jin in 661 BC.

capital:顿.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Dun, at first north of modern Shangshui; pressed by Chen, it moved south and was called Nandun. Chu destroyed Dun in 496 BC.

capital:黄.mod: NW of Huangchuan, Henan (Huang state ruins)
capital:黄.note: The Ying-surnamed state of Huang. Relying on Qi, it failed to render its dues to Chu, and Chu destroyed Huang in 648 BC.

capital:鼓.note: Capital of the White Di state of Gu (one view: the same place as Xiyang). In 527 BC Xun Wu of Jin besieged Gu for three months and took it; in 520 BC Gu rebelled, and Jin destroyed it again.

city:不羹.note: A great town on Chu's northern border, with an Eastern and a Western Bulang. In 531 BC King Ling of Chu walled Chen, Cai and Bulang, and the next year boasted that they were "each levying a thousand chariots".

city:中牟.note: A Jin town. Around 490 BC Bi Xi held Zhongmou in revolt against the Zhao lineage and invited Confucius, who wanted to go (Analects, "Yang Huo").

city:乾溪.note: Where King Ling of Chu camped while attacking Xu (530–529 BC); at home Prince Bi and Prince Qiji staged a coup, everyone abandoned the king, and he hanged himself.

city:京.note: Duke Zhuang of Zheng enfeoffed his younger brother Gongshu Duan at Jing, styled "Taishu of Jing City"; in 722 BC Duan plotted a surprise attack on Zheng, and "the earl of Zheng overcame Duan at Yan".

city:原.note: Given to Jin by Zhou in 635 BC. When the people of Yuan refused to submit, Duke Wen of Jin besieged it with three days' rations and withdrew as soon as they ran out ("attacking Yuan to show good faith"); Yuan then surrendered.

city:城父.mod: SE of Bozhou, Anhui (one view: E of Baofeng, Henan)
city:城父.note: A key northern town of Chu. In 523 BC King Ping of Chu had Crown Prince Jian live at Chengfu; Fei Wuji slandered the prince, and Wu She was killed as a result.

city:屈.note: A Jin town famed for fine horses ("the teams bred at Qu"); in the Li Ji Unrest Prince Yiwu fled to Qu.

city:平阴.note: Qi's southwestern gateway; the men of Qi dug the trench at Fangmen to its south. In 555 BC Jin led the lords against Qi, and the Qi army slipped away by night.

city:彭城.note: A Song town. In 573 BC Chu and Zheng took Pengcheng and enfeoffed the Song rebel Yu Shi there; the next year Jin led the lords to besiege and recover it.

city:戚.note: Fief of Sun Linfu, who held power in Wey; close to Jin, it was the site of many Jin–Wey covenants. In 493 BC Zhao Yang of Jin installed Kuaikui, crown prince of Wey, at Qi.

city:晋阳.note: Built by Dong Anyu on Zhao Yang's orders; the base of the Zhao lineage. In 497 BC Zhao Yang fled to Jinyang, where the Fan and Zhonghang lineages besieged him.

city:期思.note: Originally the state of Jiang; Chu destroyed it and made it Qisi County. The Chu chancellor Sunshu Ao was a rustic of Qisi and built the Qisi reservoir.

city:朱方.note: A Wu town. In 545 BC Qing Feng of Qi fled to Wu and was enfeoffed at Zhufang; in 538 BC King Ling of Chu led the lords against Wu and seized Qing Feng here.

city:栎.note: Secondary capital of Zheng. After being driven out, Duke Li of Zheng lived at Li for seventeen years (697–680 BC) and finally regained his state from here.

city:汶阳.note: Lu land on the north bank of the Wen River ("the fields of Wenyang"), repeatedly contested by Qi and Lu; after the Battle of An in 589 BC Jin ordered Qi to return it to Lu.

city:河阳.note: In the winter of 632 BC Duke Wen of Jin summoned King Xiang of Zhou here; the Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals), to avoid saying so, records that "the Heavenly King hunted at Heyang".

city:温.note: Town of the Su lineage (Ji surname). The Di destroyed Wen in 650 BC; in 635 BC King Xiang of Zhou gave Wen to Jin; in the winter of 632 BC Duke Wen of Jin assembled the lords at Wen.

city:萧.note: Xiao, a dependency of Song. King Zhuang of Chu destroyed Xiao in 597 BC; it soon reverted to Song.

city:费.note: Private town of the Jisun lineage of Lu. After Yang Hu's revolt of 502 BC, Gongshan Buniu held Bi in revolt in 498 BC, and its walls were pulled down when Confucius razed the three cities.

city:邗.note: In 486 BC Fuchai, king of Wu, "walled Han and dug a channel linking the Jiang and the Huai", to move troops and grain north in the contest for hegemony.

city:邯郸.note: Originally a Wey town, later part of Jin; the town of the Handan lineage, a cadet branch of the Zhao. In 497 BC Zhao Yang killed Handan Wu, setting off civil war among the Six Ministerial Lineages of Jin.

city:郓.note: Lu's western Yun. In 517 BC Duke Zhao of Lu, driven out by the Ji lineage, fled to Qi; the next year Qi took Yun to house Duke Zhao.

city:鄢.note: Secondary capital of Chu, named together with Ying as "Yan-Ying"; a key town on the middle Han River.

city:钟吾.mod: NE of Suqian, Jiangsu (one view: S of Xinyi)
city:钟吾.note: A small state north of the Huai. In 512 BC Helü, king of Wu, destroyed Zhongwu, and Xu the same year.

city:铜鞮.note: Site of a Jin detached palace: "the palace at Tongdi stretches for several li" (Zuozhuan, 31st year of Duke Xiang). In 514 BC the lands of the Yangshe lineage were divided into three counties, Tongdi among them.

city:阴地.note: A key place on Jin's southern frontier, where "the commissioned grandee of Yindi" was stationed to hold the hill country of western Henan; in 525 BC Jin destroyed the Luhun Rong from here.

city:高唐.note: A key town in northwestern Qi. In 554 BC Susha Wei of Qi held Gaotang in revolt and was put down by Duke Zhuang of Qi.

culture:三桓分鲁.note: The three houses of Jisun, Shusun and Mengsun "divided the ducal house into three" (562 BC) and then "into four" (537 BC), with the Ji lineage alone taking two shares; the ruler of Lu was left with an empty title.

culture:下宫之难.note: Under Duke Jing of Jin, Zhao Zhuang Ji slandered the Zhao lineage, with the Luan and Xi lineages bearing witness; Zhao Tong and Zhao Kuo were killed, but Zhao Wu survived and was later restored. This is the historical source of the "Orphan of Zhao" story.

culture:专诸刺王僚.note: Prince Guang of Wu hid armed men and invited King Liao of Wu to a feast; Zhuan Zhu, with a dagger hidden in the belly of a fish, stabbed the king to death. Guang made himself king: this was Helü.

culture:介子推隐绵山.mod: Mount Mian, SE of Jiexiu, Shanxi
culture:介子推隐绵山.note: When Duke Wen of Jin returned to his state and rewarded his followers, Jie Zitui did not ask for a stipend; he withdrew with his mother to Mianshang and died there. Duke Wen made Mianshang an estate for him, "to record my fault". The later Cold Food Festival was attached to this story.
culture:介子推隐绵山.old: Jie Zitui retires to Mount Mian

culture:伍员过昭关.note: King Ping of Chu killed Wu She and Wu Shang. Wu Yun (Zixu) fled through Song and Zheng and crossed Zhao Pass into Wu, where he helped Prince Guang seize the throne and built up Wu's army.

culture:作爰田·作州兵.note: After the defeat at Hanyuan, Jin "instituted yuantian", rewarding the people with land, and "instituted zhoubing", widening its pool of soldiers; this transformed Jin's land and military systems.

culture:侯马盟书.note: More than five thousand jade and stone tablets written in red, unearthed in 1965, record oaths between Zhao Yang and members of his lineage and his retainers, reflecting the internal struggles among the Six Ministerial Lineages of Jin.

culture:初税亩.note: Lu "first taxed land by area", levying tax per mu on all fields, public or private. This recognised private land as legitimate, and the well-field system began to break down. In 590 BC Lu also "instituted qiujia" (military levies by qiu).

culture:北杏之会.note: Duke Huan of Qi met Song, Chen, Cai and Zhu at Beixing to plan how to settle the disorder in Song. It was the first gathering of the lords presided over by Qi.

culture:卧薪尝胆.note: After the defeat at Fujiao, Goujian, king of Yue, took refuge at Kuaiji and served Wu with humble words. Back in his state he "set gall by his seat, looked up at it sitting or lying, and tasted it at every meal", employed Fan Li and Wen Zhong, and spent ten years building up his people and ten years training them (the "sleeping on brushwood" part comes from later times).
culture:卧薪尝胆.old: Sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall

culture:召陵之盟.mod: E of Yancheng District, Luohe, Henan
culture:召陵之盟.note: Duke Huan of Qi led the armies of eight states to invade Cai and attack Chu. Chu sent Qu Wan to the army: "Chu has Fangcheng for its wall and the Han River for its moat." A covenant was made at Shaoling, and the armies withdrew.

culture:堕三都.note: As minister of justice in Lu, Confucius planned to pull down the walls of Hou, Bi and Cheng, the private strongholds of the Three Huan. Hou and Bi were razed, but Cheng could not be taken and the plan failed; the next year Confucius left Lu to travel among the states.

culture:夹谷之会.mod: S of Laiwu District, Jinan, Shandong (one view: Ganyu, Jiangsu)
culture:夹谷之会.note: Qi and Lu met at Jiagu, with Confucius as master of ceremonies; invoking ritual, he drove off the Lai soldiers Qi had sent. Qi returned to Lu the lands of Yun, Huan and Guiyin.

culture:子产铸刑书.note: Zichan, in charge of the government of Zheng (from 543 BC), set field boundaries and ditches and instituted the qiu levy, then cast the penal code on a tripod, the first publication of written law; Shuxiang of Jin wrote to him in reproach.

culture:孔子.note: Confucius was born at Zouyi in Lu (around modern Mount Ni), served as minister of justice in Lu and spent fourteen years travelling among the states. Late in life he returned to Lu, edited the Odes and the Documents, compiled the Chunqiu and taught three thousand disciples. He died in 479 BC and was buried by the Si north of the Lu capital (the Kong Family Cemetery).

culture:孔子问礼于老聃.note: By tradition Confucius went to Zhou to ask Lao Dan about ritual. Laozi, a man of Li Township in Ku County in Chu, was archivist of the Zhou royal library; he wrote a book of more than five thousand characters on the meaning of the Way and virtue.
culture:孔子问礼于老聃.old: Confucius asks Lao Dan about ritual

culture:孙武吴宫教战.note: Sun Wu, a man of Qi, presented his thirteen chapters on warfare to Helü, king of Wu, and tested his drill on the palace beauties, beheading the two squad leaders. Helü then made him a general, and Wu "crushed mighty Chu to the west and overawed Qi and Jin to the north".
culture:孙武吴宫教战.old: Sun Wu's drill in the Wu palace

culture:平丘之会.note: Duke Zhao of Jin met the lords at Pingqiu and paraded four thousand armoured chariots as a show of force; Zichan argued hard to reduce Zheng's tribute. After this Jin's hegemony gradually waned.

culture:延陵季子.note: Ji Zha, a prince of Wu, repeatedly declined the throne and was enfeoffed at Yanling. In 544 BC, on a mission to Lu, he watched performances of Zhou music and commented on each part of the Feng, Ya and Song of the Odes; he also passed north through Xu and hung his sword on a tree at the tomb of the ruler of Xu.

culture:弦高犒师.note: As the Qin army passed Hua on its way to surprise Zheng, the Zheng merchant Xian Gao, falsely claiming the Zheng ruler's orders, feasted the troops with twelve oxen and sent word to Zheng. The Qin commanders, realising Zheng was ready, destroyed Hua and turned back, and on the way home were ambushed by Jin at Xiao.

culture:弭兵之会.note: At the initiative of Xiang Xu of Song, grandees from fourteen states including Jin and Chu met at Song and agreed that "the followers of Jin and Chu shall each pay court to the other"; for more than forty years afterwards there were few major wars in the Central Plains. Earlier, Hua Yuan of Song had brought about the first agreement to end war (579 BC).

culture:晋侯墓地.note: The cemetery of the Jin marquises at Beizhao has yielded nineteen tombs of nine generations of Jin marquises and their consorts; it is key evidence for locating Tang, the original fief of Jin, and its early capital.
culture:晋侯墓地.old: Cemetery of the Marquises of Jin
culture:晋侯墓地.yt: Western Zhou to early Spring and Autumn period

culture:晋铸刑鼎.note: Zhao Yang and Xun Yin of Jin levied "one gu of iron" from the people to cast penal tripods, inscribed with the penal code drawn up by Fan Xuanzi. Confucius lamented: "Jin will surely perish; it has lost its proper measure."

culture:晏婴相齐.note: Yan Ying served three rulers of Qi, Duke Ling, Duke Zhuang and Duke Jing. Frugal and diligent, he was skilled at oblique admonition; "Two peaches kill three warriors" and "Yanzi's mission to Chu" are both stories about him.

culture:曾侯與编钟.note: The inscription recalls that when the Wu army entered Ying, Zeng (Sui) "restored and secured the king of Chu", matching the Zuozhuan account of the people of Sui protecting King Zhao of Chu; it gives strong support to the view that Sui was Zeng.
culture:曾侯與编钟.old: Chime bells of Marquis Yu of Zeng

culture:柯之盟.note: Qi and Lu made a covenant at Ke. The Lu general Cao Mo (one view: the same man as Cao Gui) held Duke Huan of Qi at dagger point and forced him to return the land Qi had taken; Duke Huan did not go back on his word, and "when the lords heard of it, they all trusted Qi and wished to attach themselves to it" (the Qi Taigong chapter of the Shiji).

culture:楚县权.mod: SE of Dangyang, Hubei (one view: Jingmen)
culture:楚县权.note: King Wu of Chu destroyed Quan and appointed Dou Min "governor of Quan"; Quan is one of the earliest counties on record. Dou Min rebelled with Quan, and Chu then moved Quan to Nachu.
culture:楚县权.yt: c. the late 8th century BC (under King Wu of Chu)

culture:淅川下寺楚墓.note: Family cemetery of Prince Wu (Zigeng), chief minister of Chu. It yielded the sheng tripods of Prince Wu, a bronze altar table with cloud patterns (cast by the lost-wax method) and chime bells. The Dan–Xi area is thought to be one of the early centres of Chu activity.

culture:烛之武退秦师.note: Qin and Jin besieged Zheng. Zhu Zhiwu, a Zheng grandee, was let down the wall on a rope at night to persuade Duke Mu of Qin: "If destroying Zheng would profit you, my lord, then I would dare to trouble your officers with it." Qin made a covenant with Zheng and withdrew, leaving Qizi and others to garrison Zheng.
culture:烛之武退秦师.old: Zhu Zhiwu turns back the Qin army

culture:申包胥哭秦庭.note: When Wu entered Ying, the Chu grandee Shen Baoxu went to Qin to beg for troops: he "stood leaning against the courtyard wall and wept, his cries unbroken day and night, and for seven days not a spoonful passed his lips". Duke Ai of Qin recited the ode Wuyi ("No Clothes") for him and sent troops to save Chu.
culture:申包胥哭秦庭.old: Shen Baoxu weeps at the Qin court

culture:百里奚相秦.note: When Yu fell, Baili Xi was captured and sent to Qin as a servant in the bridal retinue of a Jin princess. He fled to Wan, where he was seized by the people of Chu; Duke Mu of Qin ransomed him for five black ram skins and entrusted him with the government, and he was called "the Five Ram Skins Grandee".

culture:秦初县邽冀.note: Duke Wu of Qin attacked the Rong of Gui and Ji and made their lands counties for the first time; the next year he also made Du and Zheng counties and destroyed Lesser Guo. These were the first counties in Qin (Basic Annals of Qin in the Shiji).
culture:秦初县邽冀.old: Qin first sets up counties at Gui and Ji

culture:章华台.note: A detached palace built by King Ling of Chu: "the whole state worked on it, and it took several years to complete". The saying "the king of Chu loved slender waists" refers to King Ling. There are large palace ruins at Longwan in Qianjiang, which one view identifies as the Zhanghua Terrace.

culture:管仲改革.note: Duke Huan of Qi made Guan Zhong his chancellor. Guan Zhong "divided the capital into three and the countryside into five", built military command into the civil administration, put the resources of mountain and sea (salt and iron) under official control, and graded taxes by the quality of the land. Qi grew rich and strong, "gathering the lords nine times and setting the realm in order".

culture:芍陂.note: By tradition built by Sunshu Ao, chancellor of Chu, it drew water from the Pi River to irrigate fields and is one of the earliest large reservoir irrigation works in China; the present-day Anfengtang reservoir is what remains of it.
culture:芍陂.yt: c. the 6th century BC (under King Zhuang of Chu)

culture:萧鱼之会.note: Duke Dao of Jin campaigned against Zheng three times, and Zheng finally submitted to Jin at a meeting at Xiaoyu. Jin returned its Zheng captives, and Zheng gave Jin female musicians and chime bells. Duke Dao restored Jin's hegemony: "within eight years he gathered the lords nine times".

culture:葵丘之会.mod: NE of Minquan, Henan (one view: Lankao)
culture:葵丘之会.note: Duke Huan of Qi met the lords at Kuiqiu, and King Xiang of Zhou sent Kong, the Steward, to present him with sacrificial meat. The covenant declared: "Do not block springs; do not stop the sale of grain; do not change the appointed heir; do not make a concubine your wife." Duke Huan's hegemony was at its peak.

culture:蔡侯申墓.mod: inside the West Gate, Shou County, Anhui
culture:蔡侯申墓.note: Tomb of Shen, Marquis Zhao of Cai. It yielded more than five hundred bronzes, including the jian basins of Guang, king of Wu, and the zun and pan of the marquis of Cai, whose inscriptions confirm Cai's marriage ties with Wu and its dependence on Wu after moving to Zhoulai.
culture:蔡侯申墓.old: Tomb of Marquis Shen of Cai

culture:虢国墓地.note: The Guo cemetery at Shangcunling has yielded the tombs of Guo Ji and Guo Zhong and large numbers of bronzes and jades, confirming that the Guo capital Shangyang lay here. Jin destroyed Guo in 655 BC.
culture:虢国墓地.old: Cemetery of the State of Guo

culture:西狩获麟.note: The people of Lu, hunting in the west at Daye, captured a qilin. Confucius sighed, "My Way has come to an end," and the Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals) he compiled breaks off here; the name "Spring and Autumn" comes from this chronicle of Lu.
culture:西狩获麟.old: Capture of the qilin on the western hunt

culture:越王勾践剑.note: The blade bears a bird-script inscription: "Jiuqian (Goujian), king of Yue, made this sword for his own use". Found in a Chu tomb, it is still sharp after more than two thousand years; it may have been part of a dowry when a Yue woman married into Chu.
culture:越王勾践剑.old: Sword of Goujian, king of Yue
culture:越王勾践剑.yt: late Spring and Autumn period (unearthed in 1965)

culture:践土之盟.note: After the Battle of Chengpu, Duke Wen of Jin built a royal palace at Jiantu and presented the Chu captives to King Xiang of Zhou, who formally appointed the marquis of Jin "leader of the lords" (hou bo). The lords made a covenant at Jiantu, and Duke Wen's hegemony was complete.

culture:鄄之会.note: Duke Huan of Qi again met Song, Chen, Wey and Zheng at Juan: "this was the beginning of Qi's hegemony" (Zuozhuan, Duke Zhuang 15).

culture:重耳出亡.note: Prince Chong'er of Jin fled from Pu and spent nineteen years among the Di and in Wey, Qi, Cao, Song, Zheng, Chu and Qin. In 636 BC Duke Mu of Qin sent him home to take the throne as Duke Wen of Jin.

culture:陈蔡之厄.note: During Confucius's travels among the states (497–484 BC), going from Chen to Cai on his way to Chu, he was trapped between Chen and Cai: "the provisions ran out, and his followers fell ill and could not rise", yet Confucius "kept lecturing, reciting, singing and playing the zither without pause".

culture:首止之会.note: Duke Huan of Qi met the lords at Shouzhi together with Zheng, crown prince of the Zhou king, to secure his position as heir. Duke Wen of Zheng, on the king's orders, slipped away without joining the covenant.

culture:骊姬之乱.note: Duke Xian of Jin doted on Li Ji. Slandered, Crown Prince Shensheng hanged himself at Xincheng (Quwo); Prince Chong'er fled to Pu and Prince Yiwu to Qu, and Jin was in turmoil for twenty years.

culture:黄池之会.note: Fuchai, king of Wu, went north to meet Duke Ding of Jin and Duke Ai of Lu at Huangchi and contended with Jin for leadership of the covenant ("Wu and Jin vied for precedence"); Yue took the chance to attack Wu and entered its capital.

pass:冥阸.mod: S of Xinyang, Henan (one view: Pingjing Pass)
pass:冥阸.note: One of the Three Passes of Yiyang. In 506 BC Xu, the Chu Marshal of the Left, planned to "block Dasui, Zhiyuan and Ming'e" to cut off the Wu retreat, but the plan came to nothing.

pass:大隧.mod: S of Luoshan, Henan (around Jiuli Pass)
pass:大隧.note: One of the Three Passes of Yiyang, on the route the Wu army took to enter Ying.

pass:太行陉.mod: Tianjing Pass, S of Jincheng, Shanxi
pass:太行陉.note: The Yangchang slope road at the southern end of the Taihang. In 550 BC Duke Zhuang of Qi attacked Jin and "climbed the Taihang", going north this way.

pass:孟津.mod: NE of Mengjin District, Luoyang, Henan
pass:孟津.note: Yellow River ford north of Chengzhou; by tradition King Wu of Zhou gathered the lords here in his campaign against King Zhou of Shang. In 525 BC Xun Wu of Jin "crossed at Jijin" to attack Luhun; one view identifies Jijin with this ford.

pass:孟门.mod: W of Huixian, Henan (around Baixing Pass)
pass:孟门.note: A pass on the southeastern flank of the Taihang. In 550 BC Duke Zhuang of Qi attacked Jin, "entering Mengmen and climbing the Taihang".

pass:少习.note: The later Wu Pass. In 491 BC Chu destroyed the Man lineage; when the viscount of Man, Chi, fled to Jin's Yindi, Chu demanded him, threatening to "open the way through Shaoxi to hear your commands", and Jin seized the viscount and handed him over to Chu.

pass:桃林塞.mod: the area from W of Lingbao, Henan to Tongguan, Shaanxi
pass:桃林塞.note: Jin's southwestern gateway. In 614 BC Jin posted Zhan Jia at Xia to guard the Taolin Pass and stop Qin from coming out to the east; it corresponds to the area of the later Hangu Pass.

pass:直辕.mod: S of Xinyang, Henan (around Wusheng Pass)
pass:直辕.note: One of the Three Passes of Yiyang, on the route the Wu army took to enter Ying.

pass:缯关.note: The northern gate of Chu's Fangcheng. In 491 BC Chu attacked the Man lineage and "gathered the men from beyond Fangcheng at Zeng Pass".

pass:茅津.note: Key Yellow River ford between Yu and Guo. In 624 BC Duke Mu of Qin "crossed at Maojin, raised a mound over the dead at Xiao and went home".

pass:蒲津.note: Yellow River ford between Qin and Jin. In 541 BC Prince Zhen of Qin fled to Jin and "built a bridge of boats on the He", the first recorded pontoon bridge over the Yellow River (one view: at this ford).

pass:虎牢.note: Zheng's stronghold "Zhi", where "Guo Shu died". In 571 BC Jin assembled the lords to wall Hulao and put pressure on Zheng, and Zheng then submitted to Jin.

pass:轘辕.mod: SE of Yanshi, Henan (NW of Dengfeng)
pass:轘辕.note: A steep road through Mount Song, the southeastern gateway of Luoyang. In 552 BC, when Luan Ying passed through Zhou on his flight to Chu, the Zhou "had the patrols escort him out through Huanyuan".

pass:阙塞.note: That is, Yique: two hills face each other with the Yi River flowing between. In 516 BC Ru Kuan of Jin held Que Pass to restore King Jing of Zhou.

pass:防门.note: Western end of the Qi Long Wall. In 555 BC Duke Ling of Qi "dug a trench at Fangmen and held it"; the Jin army set up decoy forces, and the Qi army slipped away by night.

pass:阳关.note: A fortress on Lu's northern border. In 502 BC Yang Hu seized Huan and Yang Pass in revolt; the next year Lu attacked Yang Pass, and Yang Hu fled to Qi.

people:七闽.note: Peoples of the Min region; the Zhouli speaks of the "Seven Min".

people:东胡.note: The Hu peoples north of Yan, who rose gradually after the decline of the Mountain Rong (the name Donghu appears mostly in Warring States sources).

people:代.note: A state of the northern Rong and Di, NE of modern Yu County, Hebei; destroyed by Viscount Xiang of Zhao in 457 BC.

people:北戎.note: Invaded Zheng in 714 BC and attacked Qi in 706 BC, when Crown Prince Hu of Zheng came to Qi's rescue; one view identifies them with the Mountain Rong.

people:姜戎.note: Moved by Duke Hui of Jin to Jin's southern borderland. In 627 BC they joined Jin in defeating Qin at Xiao; Juzhi, viscount of the Rong, said they had "brought them down together with Jin".

people:扬越.note: One of the Hundred Yue south of the Jiang; Xiong Qu of Chu once "attacked Yong and the Yang Yue, reaching E".

people:朝鲜.note: By tradition enfeoffed to Jizi; east of Liaodong.

people:氐.note: Lived in the mountains of southern Gansu and northern Sichuan.

people:濊貊.note: Peoples of the northeast: "the Zhui and the Mo" (Odes, Greater Odes, "Han Yi").

people:犬戎.note: In 771 BC they joined the marquis of Shen in attacking and killing King You of Zhou at the foot of Mount Li; Zongzhou was laid waste, and King Ping moved east.

people:百濮.note: Peoples southwest of the Jiang and the Han, in western Hubei and western Hunan. In 611 BC the men of Jun led the Hundred Pu to gather at Xuan, intending to attack Chu.

people:羌.note: The Western Qiang tribes, living in the He–Huang region and west of Longxi.

people:群蛮.note: Peoples of the hills southwest of Chu. In 611 BC, during a great famine in Chu, the Man tribes followed the people of Yong in revolt against Chu.

people:肃慎.note: An ancient people of the northeast, who brought Zhou tribute of "hu-wood arrows and stone arrowheads".

people:茅戎.note: Lived around Maojin. In 590 BC the Zhou royal army was routed by the Mao Rong.

people:蛮氏.note: The state of the viscount of the Rong Man, on the upper Ru River; destroyed by Chu in 491 BC.

people:西南夷.note: Peoples south of Ba and Shu.

people:长狄（鄋瞒）.note: Di of legendary great stature. In 616 BC Lu captured Qiaoru of the Tall Di, and in 607 BC Qi captured Rongru; with that the Souman perished.

people:骊戎.note: Lived around Mount Li. Duke Xian of Jin attacked the Li Rong and won Li Ji (672 BC; one view puts the Li Rong in southern Jin).

range:中条山.note: The southern screen of the Hedong basin; the "Yu slope" between Yu and Guo crossed this range (Borrowing a road to attack Guo). The salt lake lies at its northern foot.

range:五岭.note: In the Spring and Autumn far beyond the Xia states; south of the ridges was the land of the Hundred Yue.

range:伏牛山.note: The northern screen of the Nanyang basin; the Chu Fangcheng was built along its spurs: "Chu has Fangcheng for its wall".

range:会稽山.note: Birthplace of the state of Yue. In 494 BC Goujian took refuge on Kuaiji with five thousand armoured troops.

range:医巫闾山.note: The guardian mountain of ancient Youzhou; in the Spring and Autumn the land of the northeastern peoples.

range:华山.note: Anciently called Taihua, the Western Peak. Before taking power, Duke Hui of Jin promised Qin five walled towns beyond the He, reaching "south to Mount Hua".

range:南山.note: Anciently called the Nan Mountains or the Zhongnan Mountains, the southern screen of Guanzhong: "What is on Zhongnan? Catalpas and plum trees" (Odes, "Airs of Qin").

range:吕梁山.note: The western barrier of Jin; many Di (White Di and Red Di) were active in the mountains and around Xihe.

range:大别山.note: The barrier between the Yangtze and the Huai. In 506 BC the Wu army left its boats at Huairui and entered Chu through the three passes of Dasui, Zhiyuan and Ming'e.

range:大巴山.note: The barrier between Hanzhong and Ba; the Ba and Yong peoples lived to its north and south.

range:太行山.note: The barrier between Jin on one side and Wey and the Di on the other. Jin went east over the Taihang to "open up Nanyang", and later crossed the mountains to take hold of Handan and Zhaoge.

range:岷山.note: The ancients took the Min Mountains as the source of the Jiang; the birthplace of the Shu people.

range:崤山.note: The steep Xiao–Hangu route. In 627 BC Jin ambushed the Qin army here, and "not a single horse or wheel returned".

range:嵩山.note: Anciently called Taishi or Waifang, the Central Peak; between Zheng and Zhou.

range:巫山.note: Site of the Three Gorges of the Yangtze; the area of Kui and Yu was where Ba, Yong and Chu met.

range:恒山.note: The ancient Northern Peak. To its south lay Xianyu, Fei, Gu and other White Di states; to its north, Dai.

range:桐柏山.note: Source of the Huai River; the barrier to the south of Shen, Xi, Jiang, Huang and other states.

range:武夷山.note: The barrier between the Seven Min and the interior.

range:武陵山.note: Uplands of the Man tribes and the Hundred Pu, beyond Chu's southwestern frontier.

range:泰山·沂山.note: Mount Tai, anciently called Daizong, is the Eastern Peak. Qi and Lu were roughly divided by these mountains, and the Qi Long Wall was later built along their northern foot.

range:燕山.note: Yan's northern screen; the Mountain Rong roamed in and beyond the range, and Lingzhi and Guzhu lay at its southern foot. Duke Huan of Qi campaigned this far against the Mountain Rong.

range:贺兰山.note: Land of the northern Rong and Di.

range:阴山.note: In the Spring and Autumn far beyond the Xia states; the grazing lands of the northern Rong and Di.

range:陇山.note: The divide between Guanzhong and Longyou, on the route the Qin people had to take east from Xichui.

river:丹水.note: By tradition Danyang, the early Chu capital, lay between the Dan and the Xi (one view).

river:云梦泽.mod: Jianghan Plain (Honghu and nearby lakes are its remnants)
river:云梦泽.note: Hunting ground of the kings of Chu: "Yunmeng is nine hundred li square" (accounts of its extent vary). In 506 BC, when Wu entered Ying, King Zhao of Chu "waded the Ju, crossed the Jiang and entered Yun".

river:伊水.note: In 638 BC Qin and Jin moved the Luhun Rong to Yichuan.

river:圃田泽.note: A great marsh of Zheng, the Yuanpu: "Zheng has its Yuanpu as Qin has its Juyou".

river:大野泽.note: Also called the Juye Marsh, a great marsh in western Lu on the course of the Ji. In 481 BC Lu "captured a qilin on the western hunt" at Daye, and the text of the Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals) ends here.

river:大陆泽.mod: between Longyao and Julu, Hebei (silted up)
river:大陆泽.note: The ancient Julu Marsh, a great marsh of the Hebei plain. Yu Gong: "north past the Jiang River, to Dalu".

river:孟诸泽.note: A great marsh of Song. Before the Battle of Chengpu, Ziyu dreamed that the god of the He asked for his jade cap and jade tassels, promising him "the marshy shores of Mengzhu".

river:巢湖.note: The state of Chao lay near the lake; contested by Wu and Chu.

river:延江.note: Also called the Fuling River; the southern frontier of Ba.

river:彭蠡泽.note: Forerunner of modern Poyang Lake (the ancient Pengli Marsh did not cover quite the same area as the modern lake); between Wu and Chu.

river:汉水.note: Its upper course is called the Mian. Chu "has the Han River for its moat", and the Ji-surnamed states east of the Han (such as Sui) lay to its east.

river:汝水.note: Between Zheng, Xu, Cai and Chu; the line "along the banks of the Ru" comes from the Odes ("Zhou nan").

river:江.note: In the Spring and Autumn "Jiang" meant the Yangtze alone. Chu and Wu fought along it, and the Battle of Chang'an of 525 BC was fought on the river.

river:江（岷江）.note: The ancients regarded the Min River as the true source of the Yangtze; the heartland of Shu.

river:汶水.note: Border river between Qi and Lu; "the fields of Wenyang" lay on its north bank, and the two states fought over them repeatedly.

river:汾水.note: The heart of Jin: Yi, Jiang, Pingyang and Jinyang all lay on the Fen or the Kuai.

river:沁水.note: Rises in the Taiyue Mountains and flows past Jin's Nanyang (around Wen and Yuan) into the He.

river:沅水.note: Land of the Man tribes and the Hundred Pu.

river:河.note: Called simply "He" in the Spring and Autumn. The Hanshu treatise on rivers and canals quotes the Zhou pu: "in the 5th year of King Ding (602 BC) the He shifted", which many later scholars take as the first change of the lower course; but whether it shifted, and to what course, is still debated. The map keeps the Warring States lower course (schematic), reaching the sea around modern Huanghua.

river:治水.note: Also called the Lei River; its upper reaches were Dai land, and its lower course passed south of Ji, the Yan capital.

river:泗水.note: Flows south past Qufu, the Lu capital, and Pengcheng in Song into the Huai; Confucius was buried by the Si.

river:泾水.note: "The Jing is muddied by the Wei" (Odes, "Airs of Bei"); its upper reaches were the land of the Yiqu and the Quanrong.

river:洛水.note: In the area of the Qin–Jin struggle for Hexi; the Dali Rong lived on its lower course.

river:洞庭.note: In the Spring and Autumn the lake was far smaller than in later times; on Chu's southern frontier.

river:济水.note: One of the "Four Waterways": it left the He at Xingyang and flowed east, passing north of Taoqiu (the Cao capital) and through the Daye Marsh, then northeast to the sea. Wey, Cao, Lu and Qi lay largely along its banks.

river:浙江.note: Heartland of Yue; the Yue capital Kuaiji lay to its southeast.

river:淇水.note: Close to Zhaoge, the Wey capital: "Look at that bend of the Qi, its green bamboos so lush" (Odes, "Airs of Wey").

river:淮水.note: One of the "Four Waterways", flowing to the sea on its own. The states along the Huai (Jiang, Huang, Liao and Lu) fell to Chu one after another, and places such as Zhongli and Zhoulai were then fought over again and again by Wu and Chu.

river:淯水.note: Main river of the Nanyang basin, where Shen and Lü lay.

river:渭水.note: Lifeline of Guanzhong. The Qin people advanced east along the Wei, and both the Confluence of the Qian and Wei and Yong lay on its north bank.

river:湘水.note: In the Spring and Autumn Chu's power gradually reached the northern Xiang region.

river:滹沱.note: Home of Xianyu, Fei, Gu and other White Di states.

river:漳水.note: Between Jin, Wey and the Di; at the end of the Spring and Autumn the Zhao lineage of Jin developed the Zhang valley.

river:濡水.note: Land of the Mountain Rong, Lingzhi and Guzhu.

river:荥泽.note: Fed by overflow from the Ji, on Zheng's northern border; the Battle of Bi was fought to its east. In 660 BC the Di attacked Wey and "fought at Ying Marsh"; one view identifies it with this marsh.

river:菏水.note: In 482 BC Fuchai went north to the Assembly at Huangchi, "cutting a deep channel that ran through between Shang and Lu" to lead water from the He Marsh east to the Si, linking the Ji and the Si; it was later called the He River.

river:西汉水.note: Called the Xihan River in its upper course; Xichui, the early home of the Qin people, lay on its upper reaches.

river:西海.note: Ancient name of Qinghai Lake, pastureland of the Qiang.

river:豫章水.note: The "Yuzhang" where Wu and Chu fought lay north of the Jiang; the Gan River basin was then the land of the Yang Yue.

river:辽水.note: Far to the northeast of Yan; in the Spring and Autumn the land of the northeastern peoples.

river:邗沟.note: In 486 BC Fuchai, king of Wu, "walled Han and dug a channel linking the Jiang and the Huai": from Han (Yangzhou) it led water from the Jiang north through Sheyang Lake to Mokou (Huai'an) and into the Huai, to move troops and grain north in the contest for hegemony.

river:雒水.note: Both the Zhou Wangcheng and Chengzhou stood on this river; its upper reaches, between the Yi and the Luo, were home to the Rong.

river:雷夏泽.note: An ancient marsh between Wey and Cao; by tradition Shun fished in the Lei Marsh.

river:震泽.note: Modern Lake Tai, also called Juqu; the heartland of Wu.

river:颍水.note: Rises on Mount Song and flows through Zheng and Chen into the Huai.

river:饶乐水.note: Region of the Donghu and other northern peoples.

river:马訾水.note: Land of the Yemaek and Joseon.

state:东虢.note:
Capital: Zhi (around Sishui Town, modern Xingyang, Henan). Enfeoffed to Guoshu, younger brother of King Wen.
At the end of the Western Zhou Duke Huan of Zheng lodged his family between Kuai and East Guo; in 767 BC Duke Wu of Zheng destroyed East Guo, and its Hulao (Zhi) later became the key stronghold at Zheng's western gate.

state:中山.mod: Ji surname (Xianyu of the White Di)
state:中山.note:
Called Xianyu in the Spring and Autumn, a branch of the White Di, living around modern Zhengding, Hebei (Xinshi).
Jin repeatedly attacked Xianyu: it destroyed Fei, a kindred tribe, in 530 BC and Gu in 520 BC. In 506 BC the name "Zhongshan" first appears in the Zuozhuan, and thereafter Zhongshan and Xianyu are both used.
At the end of the Spring and Autumn Xianyu helped Qi and Wey attack Jin and also aided the Fan and Zhonghang lineages against Jin. In the Warring States it founded the state of Zhongshan.

state:义渠.note: One of the Western Rong, living in walled towns in what is now Qingyang in Gansu and southern Ningxia. In the Spring and Autumn it alternately fought and made peace with Qin and grew steadily stronger; in the Warring States it fought Qin for a long time and was destroyed by Qin in 272 BC.

state:伊洛之戎.note:
The Rong between the Yi and Luo rivers (the Yangju, the Quangao and the Rong of the Yi and Luo); in 649 BC, summoned by Prince Dai, they attacked and entered Wangcheng.
In 638 BC Qin and Jin moved the Luhun Rong, of the Yun surname, to Yichuan (around modern Song County and Yichuan, Henan), and from then on they were called the Luhun Rong. In 606 BC King Zhuang of Chu attacked the Luhun Rong and paraded his troops on the Zhou border; in 525 BC Xun Wu of Jin destroyed Luhun.
state:伊洛之戎.old: Rong of the Yi and Luo

state:六.note: Capital: Lu (N of modern Lu'an, Anhui). Descendants of Gaoyao. In 622 BC Lu broke with Chu and attached itself to the Eastern Yi, and Cheng Daxin and Zhong Gui of Chu led an army that destroyed Lu.

state:卫.note:
Capitals: Zhaoge → Caoyi (660 BC) → Chuqiu (658 BC) → Diqiu (Puyang, 629 BC). Enfeoffed to Kang Shu, younger brother of King Wu, in the old lands of Yin-Shang.
Duke Yi loved cranes; when the Di attacked Wey in 660 BC, the people said, "Send the cranes: the cranes have the ranks and stipends; how can we fight?" The Wey army was routed, Duke Yi was killed and the state all but perished; the survivors crossed the river and set up Duke Dai at Caoyi. Duke Huan of Qi led the lords in walling Chuqiu to re-establish Wey, and "Wey forgot it had been lost".
Duke Wen revived the state and destroyed Xing in 635 BC. Thereafter Wey was wedged between Jin and Qi, and its old lands at Zhaoge and in Henei gradually passed to Jin.
Ji Zha said, "Wey has many gentlemen; it will come to no harm"; Confucius stayed longer in Wey than anywhere else, and Duke Ling of Wey, Nanzi and the Kuaikui troubles all belong to the end of the Spring and Autumn.
