state:古魏.note:
Capital: Wei (N of modern Ruicheng, Shanxi). The Wei of the Ji surname enfeoffed in the early Western Zhou, called "Old Wei" on the map to distinguish it from the Wei of the Warring States.
In 661 BC Duke Xian of Jin destroyed Wei and granted its land to the grandee Bi Wan: the Wei lineage of the Three Jin took its name from here.

state:吴.note:
Capital: Wu (Helü's Great City, modern Suzhou, Jiangsu; one view puts Wu's early capital at Meili, in modern Wuxi). Founded by Taibo and Zhongyong, who fled to the Jing Man; it called itself Gouwu.
In 584 BC Wuchen, Duke of Shen, an exile from Chu, came to Wu as an envoy from Jin and taught the people of Wu chariot driving, archery and battle formations; Wu began to attack Chu and entered Zhoulai, and Shoumeng took the title of king.
Helü (514–496 BC) employed Wu Zixu and Sun Wu, destroyed Xu and Zhongwu (512 BC), and after the Battle of Baiju fought his way into Ying in five battles (506 BC); wounded in the foot at the Battle of Zuili, he died.
Fuchai defeated Yue at Fujiao (494 BC), cut the Hangou Canal and the He River to push north, routed the Qi army at Ailing (484 BC) and contested precedence with Jin at Huangchi (482 BC). Yue struck Wu while it was undefended; Wu was defeated again at Li Marsh in 478 BC, from 475 BC Yue besieged Wu, and in 473 BC Wu fell.

state:周（王畿）.note:
Capital: Luoyi (Wangcheng, modern Luoyang, Henan). In 771 BC the marquis of Shen joined the Quanrong in attacking and killing King You below Mount Li; in 770 BC King Ping moved the capital east to Luoyi, the start of what is known as the Eastern Zhou.
Just after the move east the royal domain still held the lands of the Yi and Luo and of Henei, which were later granted away piece by piece to Zheng, Qin and Jin; in 635 BC King Xiang granted the lands of Yangfan, Wen, Yuan and Cuanmao to Duke Wen of Jin, leaving the royal house with only the area around Luoyang.
In 707 BC King Huan led the lords against Zheng and was defeated at the Battle of Xuge; "Zhu Dan shot the king in the shoulder", and the prestige of the royal house was shattered.
The lords contended for hegemony in the name of "revering the king and expelling the barbarians", and Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin were in turn invested as leader of the lords (houbo). In 606 BC King Zhuang of Chu paraded his troops on the Zhou border and asked about the size and weight of the tripods; Wangsun Man replied that "it lies in virtue, not in the tripods".
The royal house suffered repeated internal strife: the rebellion of Prince Tui (675 BC), the rebellion of Prince Dai (649 and 636 BC) and the rebellion of Prince Zhao (520–516 BC); Prince Zhao fled to Chu, taking the records of the Zhou house with him.

state:唐.note: Capital: Tang (Tangxian Town, NW of modern Suizhou, Hubei). Duke Cheng of Tang was detained for three years for refusing to give horses to the Chu chief minister Zichang, and so joined Cai in bringing Wu to attack Chu (506 BC). In 505 BC, after Chu was restored, it destroyed Tang.

state:大荔.note: The Dali Rong lived around modern Dali, Shaanxi, built a royal city (Wangcheng) and styled their ruler king. At the end of the Spring and Autumn they held out against Qin; in 461 BC Duke Ligong of Qin attacked Dali with twenty thousand troops and took its Wangcheng (later renamed Linjin).

state:宋.mod: Zi surname (descendants of the Shang kings)
state:宋.note:
Capital: Shangqiu (Suiyang). Enfeoffed to Weizi; the Zhou treated Song with the rites due to a "guest", and its ruler ranked as a duke.
Duke Xiang (650–637 BC) sought hegemony but was seized by Chu at the Assembly at Yu (639 BC); at the Battle of Hong (638 BC) he "would not drum the attack on an enemy not yet in formation", and was wounded in the thigh and died.
In 595–594 BC King Zhuang of Chu besieged Song for nine months; inside the city "they exchanged children to eat and split bones for firewood"; Hua Yuan slipped into the Chu camp by night, and Song made peace with Chu.
The two assemblies to end war, in 579 and 546 BC, were both initiated by men of Song (Hua Yuan and Xiang Xu); at the second, Jin and Chu shared the leadership of the covenant.
In 487 BC Duke Jing destroyed Cao, extending Song's territory to Taoqiu. People: Hua Yuan, Xiang Xu, Zihan; according to one view, Mozi was also from Song.

state:山戎.note: Also called the Northern Rong, living around the Yan Mountains in modern northern Hebei; Lingzhi and others belonged to them. In 714 BC the Northern Rong raided Zheng, and in 706 BC they attacked Qi. In 664 BC the Mountain Rong attacked Yan; Duke Huan of Qi marched north, "struck Lingzhi and cut down Guzhu", and returned. After this they are no longer drawn on the map.

state:巢.note: Capital: Chao (NE of modern Chaohu, Anhui; one view: around Wabu Lake). A small state between Wu and Chu, subject to Chu. In 548 BC Zhufan, king of Wu, attacked Chu and assaulted the gate of Chao, where he was hit by an arrow from Niu Chen of Chao and died; Wu destroyed Chao in 518 BC.

state:巴.mod: Ji surname (one view: descendants of Lord Lin)
state:巴.note:
In the Spring and Autumn the state of Ba lay roughly on the upper Han River, north and south of the Daba Mountains (location disputed). In 703 BC the viscount of Ba sent Han Fu to Chu, "asking to establish friendly relations with Deng"; thereafter it was sometimes at war and sometimes at peace with Chu, and it joined Chu and Qin in destroying Yong (611 BC).
In the middle and late Spring and Autumn it gradually moved south, and in the Warring States it was centred on Jiangzhou (modern Chongqing).

state:庸.note:
Capital: Shangyong (SW of modern Zhushan, Hubei). It once joined King Wu in attacking the Shang king Zhou: one of the "men of Yong, Shu, Qiang, Mao, Wei, Lu, Peng and Pu".
In 611 BC, during a great famine in Chu, the people of Yong led the Man tribes, and the people of Jun the Hundred Pu, in revolt against Chu; King Zhuang of Chu joined with Qin and Ba to destroy Yong, and its land passed to Chu.

state:徐.note:
Capital: Xu (Daxucheng, S of modern Sihong, Jiangsu). Descendants of Boyi; by tradition King Yan of Xu practised benevolence and righteousness in the Western Zhou, and "thirty-six states came overland to pay him court".
In the Spring and Autumn a great state of the Huai Yi, repeatedly attacked by Qi, Chu and Wu; in 512 BC Helü, king of Wu, "dammed the hills to flood it" and destroyed Xu, and Zhangyu, viscount of Xu, fled to Chu.

state:息.note: Capital: Xi (SW of modern Xi County, Henan). Xi Gui, wife of the marquis of Xi, was insulted when passing through Cai, and the marquis of Xi led Chu to attack Cai (684 BC); Marquis Ai of Cai in turn praised Xi Gui's beauty to the king of Chu, and King Wen of Chu destroyed Xi (680 BC) and took Xi Gui, who bore him Du'ao and King Cheng.

state:晋.note:
Capitals: Yi (Old Jiang, around modern Yicheng, Shanxi) → Jiang (walled by Duke Xian in 669 BC) → Xintian (modern Houma, Shanxi; moved there by Duke Jing in 585 BC, still called Jiang, also New Jiang).
In 745 BC Marquis Zhao enfeoffed his uncle Chengshi at Quwo, and the cadet branch fought the senior line for sixty-seven years; in 678 BC Duke Wu of Quwo destroyed Yi and was invested as marquis of Jin.
Duke Xian (676–651 BC) "annexed seventeen states and subjugated thirty-eight": he destroyed Huo, Wei and Geng (661 BC) and, borrowing a road through Yu, destroyed Guo and Yu (655 BC). After the Li Ji Unrest, Prince Chong'er spent nineteen years in exile.
Duke Wen (636–628 BC) came to the king's aid and gained Nanyang, defeated Chu at Chengpu (632 BC) and was invested as leader of the lords (houbo) at the Covenant of Jiantu. For more than a century thereafter Jin presided over the covenants and assemblies of the Central Plains: defeat at Bi (597 BC), victory at An (589 BC), victory at Yanling (575 BC), Duke Dao regaining hegemony (562 BC).
Duke Jing destroyed the Red Di (594–588 BC); under Dukes Zhao and Qing, Jin also destroyed Fei, Luhun and Gu.
Power passed gradually to the Six Ministerial Lineages: in 497–490 BC the Fan and Zhonghang lineages were defeated and destroyed, the four ministerial lineages of Zhi, Zhao, Han and Wei divided Jin among themselves, and by the end of the Spring and Autumn the ruler of Jin reigned in name only.

state:曲沃.note:
Capital: Quwo (E of modern Wenxi, Shanxi). In 745 BC Marquis Zhao of Jin enfeoffed his uncle Chengshi (Huan Shu) at Quwo, a town larger than the capital at Yi: "the branch larger than the root".
Over three generations, Huan Shu, Zhuangbo and Duke Wu fought the ruling house at Yi for sixty-seven years, killing several of its rulers in turn. In 678 BC Duke Wu of Quwo destroyed Yi, bribed King Xi of Zhou with treasures and was invested as marquis of Jin, and Jin was reunited under the Quwo line.

state:曹.note:
Capital: Taoqiu (modern Dingtao District, Heze, Shandong). Enfeoffed to Shu Zhenduo, younger brother of King Wu; a small state lying between Song, Wey and Lu.
When Chong'er passed through Cao in exile, Duke Gong of Cao spied on his fused ribs; in 632 BC Duke Wen of Jin attacked Cao, entered its capital and seized Duke Gong. In the Spring and Autumn Cao mostly followed Jin.
In 487 BC Duke Jing of Song destroyed Cao and carried off Yang, earl of Cao.

state:杞.note:
Capitals: Yongqiu (modern Qi County, Henan) → moved east into Shandong (early Spring and Autumn) → Yuanling (646 BC; SE of modern Changle, Shandong) → Chunyu (544 BC; NE of modern Anqiu, Shandong). Descendants of Yu of Xia.
Small and weak, it was repeatedly harassed by the Huai Yi, Ju and Lu; Duke Huan of Qi led the lords in walling Yuanling and moved it there, and Duke Ping of Jin in turn led the lords in walling Chunyu. Confucius lamented that "Qi does not furnish enough evidence".
Destroyed by King Hui of Chu in 445 BC.

state:梁.note:
Capital: Shaoliang (S of modern Hancheng, Shaanxi). Of the Ying surname, like Qin.
The earl of Liang loved building works, "walling towns again and again without settling them, until the people were exhausted and could bear no more"; in 641 BC Qin took Liang when its people scattered. Its land later became Shaoliang, the key Hexi stronghold fought over again and again by Qin and Jin, and by Qin and Wei.

state:楚.note:
Capitals: Danyang (location disputed) → Ying (first made the capital by King Wen in 689 BC; generally placed around Jinancheng in modern Jingzhou, Hubei, though scholars still debate where the Spring and Autumn Ying lay); in 504 BC King Zhao, to escape Wu, moved the capital to Ruo for a time.
In the Western Zhou it lay remote in the Jing Mountains, "in rough carts and ragged clothes opening up the hills and forests". In 704 BC Xiong Tong proclaimed himself King Wu, attacked Sui and destroyed Quan; King Wen destroyed Shen, Xi and Deng and pushed north beyond Fangcheng.
King Cheng made a covenant with Duke Huan of Qi at Shaoling (656 BC), defeated Duke Xiang of Song at the Hong (638 BC) and was defeated at Chengpu (632 BC). King Zhuang (613–591 BC) destroyed Yong, asked about the tripods of the Central Plains, routed the Jin army at the Battle of Bi and became hegemon.
King Gong was defeated by Jin at Yanling (575 BC). King Ling destroyed Chen and Cai (534 and 531 BC) and hanged himself after the revolt at Ganxi; King Ping restored Chen and Cai.
In 506 BC the Wu army fought five battles and entered Ying; King Zhao fled, and Shen Baoxu begged Qin for an army to restore the state. King Hui destroyed Chen (478 BC).
Chu annexed more states than any other in the Spring and Autumn: "of the Ji states north of the Han, Chu has swallowed them all"; Shen, Xi, Deng, Huang, Jiang, Lu, Liao, Yong, Qunshu, Tang, Dun, Hu and others all passed to Chu, most of them governed as counties.

state:江.note: Capital: Jiang (SE of modern Zhengyang, Henan). Like Huang it attached itself to Duke Huan of Qi. Destroyed by King Mu of Chu in 623 BC; Duke Mu of Qin put on plain mourning clothes and moved out of his chambers for it.

state:沈.note: Capital: Shen (N of modern Pingyu, Henan). A Chu dependency. In 506 BC Shen did not attend the Assembly at Shaoling, so Jin had Cai attack Shen; Cai destroyed Shen and killed Jia, viscount of Shen.

state:淮夷.note: The Eastern Yi tribes of the middle and lower Huai River, in what is now northern Jiangsu. They repeatedly harassed Qi and Zeng, and for this reason Duke Huan of Qi led the lords in walling Yuanling to move Qi there (646 BC) and assembled the lords at the Huai (644 BC). In 538 BC the Huai Yi also attended King Ling of Chu's Assembly at Shen; afterwards they were gradually absorbed by Wu and Chu.

state:滑.note:
Capital: Fei (Goushi Town, modern Yanshi, Henan). A small state between Zhou and Zheng, wavering between Zheng and Wey.
In 627 BC a Qin army marching to surprise Zheng reached Hua and met the Zheng merchant Xian Gao, who feasted the troops; realising that Zheng was prepared, the Qin destroyed Hua and turned back, and on the way home the army was wiped out by Jin at Xiao. The land of Hua later passed to Jin.

state:滕.note:
Capital: Teng (SW of modern Tengzhou, Shandong). Enfeoffed to Cuo Shu Xiu, a son of King Wen. One of the small states on the Si; in the Spring and Autumn it mostly followed Lu and Song and paid court to Jin.
In the Warring States Duke Wen of Teng asked Mencius about government (c. 326 BC); Teng was later destroyed by Song.

state:燕.note:
Capital: Ji (SW of modern Beijing). Enfeoffed to Shi, Duke of Shao.
In the Spring and Autumn it lay remote in the north, had little contact with the lords of the Central Plains, and was repeatedly raided by the Mountain Rong. In 664 BC the Mountain Rong attacked Yan; Duke Huan of Qi marched north against them, going as far as Guzhu before turning back. Duke Zhuang of Yan escorted Duke Huan into Qi territory, and Duke Huan ceded to Yan the land as far as the ruler of Yan had come, so that Yan might "restore the laws of the Duke of Shao".
The history of Yan in the Spring and Autumn is fragmentary; the Yan chapter of the Shiji records little more than its line of rulers.

state:申.note:
Capital: Shen (around Wancheng District, modern Nanyang, Henan). Enfeoffed to the earl of Shen, maternal uncle of King Xuan (at Xie), to shield the southern lands; a marquis of Shen joined the Quanrong in attacking and killing King You and set up his daughter's son, King Ping.
Destroyed by King Wen of Chu around 688 BC and made the county of Shen; the levies of Shen and Lü became the mainstay of Chu's defence against the north.

state:白狄.note:
Lived around Xihe (modern northern Shaanxi and northwestern Shanxi) and later moved east into central Hebei; their states included Xianyu, Fei, Gu and Qiuyou. They alternately fought and made peace with Jin; Prince Chong'er spent twelve years among the Di during his exile.
Jin destroyed Fei in 530 BC and Gu in 520 BC; Xianyu later founded the state of Zhongshan.

state:秦.note:
Capitals: Xichui (Quanqiu) → Confluence of the Qian and Wei (762 BC) → Pingyang (714 BC) → Yong (677 BC).
In the Western Zhou a dependency that bred horses for the Zhou king. In 770 BC Duke Xiang escorted King Ping on his move east, and Qin was first ranked among the feudal lords; King Ping promised it "the land west of Mount Qi", which Qin had to win by driving out the Rong itself: Duke Wen defeated the Rong and took in the remaining Zhou people (750 BC), and Duke Wu attacked the Rong of Gui and Ji and first set up counties (688 BC).
Duke Mu (659–621 BC) employed Baili Xi, Jian Shu and You Yu: he captured Duke Hui of Jin at the Battle of Hanyuan (645 BC) and gained Jin's Hexi; destroyed Liang and Rui (641 and 640 BC); and, after his advance east was checked at Xiao (627 BC), turned west, "adding twelve states and opening up a thousand li of land, and so became hegemon of the Western Rong" (623 BC).
Thereafter Qin and Jin long contested Hexi; remote in Yongzhou, Qin rarely joined the covenants and assemblies of the Central Plains. In 505 BC Duke Ai sent five hundred chariots to rescue Chu and defeated Wu.

state:纪.note:
Capital: Ji (Jitai, S of modern Shouguang, Shandong). Of the Jiang surname like Qi; by tradition a marquis of Ji slandered Duke Ai of Qi to the Zhou king, who had Duke Ai boiled.
Duke Xiang of Qi attacked Ji on the pretext of avenging a wrong done nine generations before; in 690 BC the marquis of Ji "left his state for good", and Ji fell to Qi.

state:群舒.note:
Shu, Shuyong, Shuliao, Shujiu, Shulong, Shubao, Shugong and other small states of the Yan surname, scattered around modern Shucheng, Lujiang and Tongcheng in Anhui, between Wu and Chu.
In 657 BC Xu took Shu; King Zhuang of Chu destroyed Shuliao (601 BC), Chu destroyed Shuyong in 574 BC and Shujiu in 548 BC, and all of Qunshu passed to Chu.

state:耿.note: Capital: Geng (SE of modern Hejin, Shanxi). In 661 BC Duke Xian of Jin destroyed Geng and granted its land to the grandee Zhao Su: the first fief of the Zhao lineage in Jin.

state:胡.note: Capital: Hu (NW of modern Fuyang, Anhui). A small state on the Huai and a Chu dependency. In 506 BC, when Wu entered Ying, the viscount of Hu carried off all the people of the Chu towns near Hu; in 495 BC King Zhao of Chu destroyed Hu and seized Bao, viscount of Hu.

state:芮.note:
Capital: Rui (around Chaoyi Town, modern Dali, Shaanxi; the large Rui tombs at Liangdai Village, Hancheng, may mark its earlier seat). An old state of the Western Zhou. In 709 BC Wan, earl of Rui, was driven out by his mother Rui Jiang and went to live in Wei.
Wedged between Qin and Jin, it was destroyed by Duke Mu of Qin in 640 BC.

state:莒.note:
Capital: Ju (modern Ju County, Shandong). An ancient state of the Eastern Yi and one of the stronger states of the east in the Spring and Autumn; it contested Yun with Lu and destroyed Zeng in 567 BC.
Prince Xiaobai of Qi (Duke Huan) once took refuge in Ju. Destroyed by King Jian of Chu in 431 BC; its land later passed to Qi and became one of Qi's "Five Capitals".

state:莱.note:
Capital: Lai (the Guicheng ruins, SE of modern Longkou, Shandong; one view: around Changle). A great state of the Eastern Yi, holding the Jiaodong Peninsula with its wealth in fish and salt.
When Taigong was first enfeoffed at Yingqiu, "the marquis of Lai came to attack and contested Yingqiu with him". In 567 BC Duke Ling of Qi destroyed Lai and moved Lai to Ni, and Qi held the whole of Jiaodong.

state:蓼.note: Capital: Liao (NE of modern Gushi, Henan). In 622 BC Chu destroyed Lu and Liao, and Zang Wenzhong of Lu sighed: "So Gaoyao and Tingjian are suddenly left without sacrifices!"

state:蔡.note:
Capitals: Shangcai → Xincai (moved there after the restoration of 529 BC) → Zhoulai (Xiacai, modern Fengtai, Anhui; moved there in 493 BC). Enfeoffed to Shu Du, younger brother of King Wu.
Wedged between Chu, Chen and Zheng, it was long a dependency of Chu. In 684 BC Chu defeated Cai at Shen and captured Marquis Ai. In 531 BC King Ling of Chu lured Marquis Ling to his death and made Cai a county; in 529 BC King Ping restored it.
Marquis Zhao of Cai, extorted by the Chu chief minister Zichang, brought in Wu to attack Chu, and after the Battle of Baiju in 506 BC Wu entered Ying; the same year Cai destroyed Shen. Thereafter, fearing Chu, Cai moved to Zhoulai to rely on Wu.
King Hui of Chu destroyed Cai in 447 BC.

state:薛.note:
Capital: Xue (the Xue state ruins at Guanqiao Town, SE of modern Tengzhou, Shandong). Descendants of Xi Zhong, who by tradition was master of chariots under the Xia and first made carts.
In the Spring and Autumn, like Teng and Zhu, a small state on the Si. Annexed by Qi in the early Warring States (date unknown); in 321 BC Qi enfeoffed Tian Ying at Xue, and his son was Tian Wen, Lord Mengchang.

state:虞.note:
Capital: Yu (N of modern Pinglu, Shanxi). Enfeoffed to Yuzhong, a descendant of Taibo and Zhongyong.
Duke Xian of Jin, offering horses bred at Qu and jade discs from Chuiji, twice asked Yu for passage to attack Guo; Gong Zhiqi remonstrated that "when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold", but the duke of Yu would not listen. In 655 BC Jin destroyed Guo, fell on Yu on the way back and seized the duke of Yu; the grandee Baili Xi was taken captive to Jin and later became chancellor of Qin.

state:虢.note:
Capital: Shangyang (modern Sanmenxia, Henan); on the north bank of the Yellow River lay Xiayang (NE of modern Pinglu, Shanxi). West Guo moved east to here and straddled the river, so it was known as both South Guo and North Guo.
The dukes of Guo were hereditary ministers of the Zhou king and once led the royal army against Quwo. In 658 BC Jin borrowed a road through Yu and took Xiayang; in 655 BC it borrowed the road again, besieged Shangyang and destroyed Guo: this is the origin of "when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold".

state:蜀.note:
The ancient state of Shu, centred on the Chengdu Plain; the Sanxingdui and Jinsha sites represent the civilisation of its forerunners.
In the Spring and Autumn it had little contact with the Central Plains; by legend, after Duyu (Emperor Wang), Bieling, who had tamed the floods, received the throne by abdication and became the Kaiming lineage.

state:西戎.note:
The Rong in and around the Long Mountains: the Quanrong, the Rong of Gui and Ji, Mianzhu, the Gun Rong, Di, Huan, the Pengxi lineage and others. In 771 BC the Quanrong attacked and killed King You below Mount Li.
Dukes Xiang, Wen, Ning and Wu of Qin drove out the Rong and extended their territory: in 688 BC Duke Wu of Qin attacked the Rong of Gui and Ji and first made their lands counties. In 623 BC Duke Mu of Qin, following You Yu's counsel, "added twelve states, opened up a thousand li of land, and became hegemon of the Western Rong", and most of the Rong submitted to Qin.

state:许.note:
Capitals: Xu (E of modern Xuchang, Henan) → She (576 BC) → Yi (533 BC) → She (529 BC) → Baiyu (524 BC) → Rongcheng (506 BC). Descended from Boyi, the Taiyue.
Wedged between Zheng and Chu: in 712 BC Duke Zhuang of Zheng entered Xu together with Qi and Lu. To escape pressure from Zheng the rulers of Xu moved again and again, ending up as a Chu dependency. In 504 BC Zheng destroyed Xu, but Xu was soon restored.
It fell early in the Warring States, whether to Chu or to Wei, at an unknown date.

state:谭.note: Capital: Tan (around Longshan Town, Zhangqiu District, modern Jinan, Shandong). When Duke Huan of Qi passed through Tan in exile, Tan showed him no courtesy; when he came to the throne and the lords all sent congratulations, Tan again did not come. In 684 BC Qi destroyed Tan, and the viscount of Tan fled to Ju.

state:赤狄.note:
Lived around Shangdang at the western foot of the Taihang Mountains; its groups included the Lu lineage, the Jia lineage, Liuxu, Duochen, the Dongshan Gaoluo lineage and Qianggaoru. Strongest in the early Spring and Autumn: they attacked Xing in 662–661 BC and destroyed Wey in 660 BC, and they repeatedly raided Jin and Zhou.
In 594 BC Xun Linfu of Jin destroyed the Lu lineage; in 593 BC Shi Hui destroyed the Jia lineage and Liuxu; in 588 BC Qianggaoru was destroyed, and all the Red Di passed to Jin.

state:越.note:
Capital: Kuaiji (modern Shaoxing, Zhejiang). It claimed descent from Wuyu, a son of Shaokang of Xia by a secondary consort; its people cut their hair short and tattooed their bodies.
At the end of the Spring and Autumn Yunchang first took the title of king; Yue and Wu were hereditary enemies. In 496 BC Goujian defeated Wu at Zuili, and Helü died of his wound; after the defeat at Fujiao in 494 BC Goujian went to Wu as a vassal, and on returning home he slept on brushwood and tasted gall, and with Fan Li and Wen Zhong spent "ten years building up the people and their wealth, and ten years teaching and training them".
In 482 BC, while Fuchai was away in the north at the Assembly at Huangchi, Yue fell on the Wu capital; in 478 BC it routed the Wu army at Li Marsh; from 475 BC it besieged Wu for three years, and in 473 BC it destroyed Wu.

state:遂.note: Capital: Sui (NW of modern Ningyang, Shandong). Descendants of Shun. In 681 BC Duke Huan of Qi assembled the lords at Beixing; the men of Sui did not come, so Qi destroyed Sui and garrisoned it; in 677 BC the men of Sui killed the entire Qi garrison.

state:邓.note:
Capital: Deng (the Dengcheng ruins, Fancheng District, modern Xiangyang, Hubei; one view: Dengzhou, Henan). Deng Man, wife of King Wu of Chu, was a daughter of Deng.
In 688 BC King Wen of Chu passed through Deng on his way to attack Shen; the three nephews of Deng urged that he be killed, but Marquis Qi of Deng refused. Chu destroyed Deng in 678 BC.

state:邢.note:
Capitals: Xing (modern Xingtai, Hebei) → Yiyi (659 BC; SW of modern Liaocheng, Shandong; one view: W of Xingtai, Hebei). Enfeoffed to a son of the Duke of Zhou.
In 662–661 BC the Di attacked Xing; Duke Huan of Qi came to its rescue and in 659 BC moved Xing to Yiyi, and "Xing moved as if coming home".
Duke Wen of Wey destroyed Xing in 635 BC.

state:邾.note:
Capitals: Zhu → Yi (614 BC; the Jiwangcheng ruins south of Mount Yi, modern Zoucheng, Shandong). Descendants of Zhuanxu; called Zou in the Warring States.
Bordering Lu, it fought Lu for generations: "the watchmen's clappers of Lu can be heard in Zhu". Duke Wen of Zhu, divining about a move to Yi, said: "My mandate lies in nourishing the people; whether my death comes early or late is a matter of time."
In the Warring States it was the state of Zou; Mencius was a man of Zou.

state:郐.note: Capital: Kuai (SE of modern Xinmi, Henan). Descendants of Zhurong. Duke Wu of Zheng destroyed Kuai in 769 BC. The "Airs of Kuai" in the Shijing are the songs of Kuai; when Ji Zha listened to the music of the states, "from Kuai on he made no comment".

state:郑.note:
Capital: Xinzheng (from 767 BC; in the Spring and Autumn simply called "Zheng"). King Xuan enfeoffed his younger brother You (Duke Huan) at Zheng (around modern Huazhou District, Weinan, Shaanxi); at the end of the Western Zhou Duke Huan lodged his family between Kuai and East Guo, and Duke Wu destroyed Kuai (769 BC) and East Guo (767 BC) and founded the state east of the He and the Luo.
Duke Zhuang (743–701 BC) defeated Duan at Yan and defeated King Huan of Zhou at the Battle of Xuge, and was called the "lesser hegemon".
Lying at "the centre of the realm", with Jin to the north and Chu to the south, Zheng sided with Jin in the morning and Chu in the evening, and suffered more Jin and Chu invasions than any other state in the Spring and Autumn: the Battles of Bi (597 BC) and Yanling (575 BC) both arose over Zheng; after the Assembly at Xiaoyu in 562 BC it went over to Jin.
Zichan governed the state (543–522 BC), instituted the qiu levy and cast the penal code (536 BC), and "did not close the village schools"; under him Zheng, a small state, held its own between Jin and Chu.
Destroyed by Han in 375 BC.

state:郯.note:
Capital: Tan (N of modern Tancheng, Shandong). An ancient state of the Eastern Yi. In 525 BC the viscount of Tan visited the Lu court and, answering a question from Shusun Zhaozi, explained how Shaohao had named his officials after birds; Confucius heard of it and went to learn from him, sighing that "when the Son of Heaven has lost his offices, learning survives among the four Yi".
Destroyed by Yue around 414 BC.

state:鄫.note: Capital: Zeng (E of Yicheng District, modern Zaozhuang, Shandong). Descendants of Yu of Xia, wedged between Lu and Ju. In 641 BC Duke Xiang of Song had Duke Wen of Zhu sacrifice the viscount of Zeng at the altar of Cisui, using a man as the offering. Destroyed by Ju in 567 BC.

state:钟离.note: Capital: Zhongli (Linhuaiguan, NE of modern Fengyang, Anhui). A small state on the Wu–Chu border. In 518 BC women of the Wu border town of Beiliang and the Chu border town of Zhongli quarrelled over mulberry leaves, the two states went to war, and Wu destroyed Zhongli and Chao.

state:陈.note:
Capital: Wanqiu (modern Huaiyang District, Zhoukou, Henan). Enfeoffed to Duke Hu Man, a descendant of Shun.
Lying at Chu's northern gate, it suffered repeated Chu invasions once Chu rose. In 599 BC Xia Zhengshu killed Duke Ling; the next year King Zhuang of Chu entered Chen and briefly made it a county, but soon restored it.
In 534 BC King Ling of Chu destroyed Chen and made it a county; in 529 BC King Ping restored it. Prince Wan of Chen fled to Qi in 672 BC: he was the ancestor of the Tian lineage.
Confucius was once "in distress between Chen and Cai" (489 BC). In 478 BC King Hui of Chu killed Duke Min of Chen, and Chen fell.

state:随.note:
Capital: Sui (modern Suizhou, Hubei). Leader of the Ji states east of the Han: "of the states east of the Han, Sui is the greatest". The state of Zeng known from archaeology is Sui, and the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng (c. 433 BC) is the tomb of one of its rulers.
King Wu of Chu attacked Sui three times (706, 704 and 690 BC), and Sui submitted to Chu. In 506 BC King Zhao of Chu fled from Wu to Sui, and the people of Sui refused to hand him over.
Absorbed by Chu in the early Warring States, at an unknown date.

state:霍.note: Capital: Huo (SW of modern Huozhou, Shanxi). Enfeoffed to Huo Shu Chu, younger brother of King Wu, one of the "Three Overseers". Destroyed by Duke Xian of Jin in 661 BC; Mount Huotai (modern Mount Huo) takes its name from the state.

state:顿.note: Capital: Dun (W of modern Xiangcheng, Henan; one view: Shangshui). Repeatedly pressed by Chen, it relied on Chu. Chu destroyed Dun in 496 BC.

state:鲁.note:
Capital: Qufu. First enfeoffed to Boqin, son of the Duke of Zhou; "the rites of Zhou are all in Lu".
The Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals) is the chronicle of Lu, running from the first year of Duke Yin (722 BC) to the fourteenth year of Duke Ai (481 BC), ending with the "capture of the qilin on the western hunt".
Under Duke Zhuang, Cao Gui gave his counsel on battle, and Lu defeated Qi at Changshao (684 BC). From Duke Xi onward Lu relied on Qi and Jin. In 594 BC Duke Xuan introduced the "first land tax by area" (chushuimu), taxing land by acreage and so recognising private fields.
Power passed to the "Three Huan", the Jisun, Shusun and Mengsun: in 562 BC they divided the ducal domain into three, in 537 BC into four; Duke Zhao's attack on the Jisun failed, and he fled to Qi and died in exile at Ganhou.
Confucius (551–479 BC) served as minister of crime of Lu; in 498 BC he led the "razing of the three cities", which failed; after fourteen years travelling among the states he returned to Lu and edited and transmitted the Six Classics.

state:黄.note: Capital: Huang (the Huang state ruins, NW of modern Huangchuan, Henan). Relying on support from Qi, it did not serve Chu, saying, "From Ying to us is nine hundred li; how can they harm us?" Chu destroyed Huang in 648 BC.

state:齐.note:
Capital: Linzi (Yingqiu). First enfeoffed to Taigong Wang, who "promoted the work of merchants and artisans and made the most of fish and salt".
Duke Xiang destroyed Ji (690 BC). Duke Huan (685–643 BC) made Guan Zhong his chancellor and "assembled the lords nine times and set all under Heaven in order": he attacked the Mountain Rong in the north to rescue Yan (664–663 BC), preserved Xing and re-established Wey (659–658 BC), attacked Chu in the south and made a covenant at Shaoling (656 BC), and held a great assembly of the lords at Kuiqiu (651 BC), becoming the first hegemon of the Spring and Autumn; he also destroyed Tan, Sui and Zhang.
After Duke Huan's death five of his sons fought over the succession, and Qi's hegemony faded. Duke Qing was defeated at An (589 BC); Duke Ling destroyed Lai (567 BC) and took the whole of Jiaodong.
Under Duke Jing, Yan Ying was chancellor. Prince Wan of Chen fled to Qi, and his line became the Tian lineage, which won people's hearts by lending with a large measure and collecting with a small one; in 481 BC Tian Chang killed Duke Jian and took control of the government of Qi: the usurpation of Qi by Tian began here.
People: Guan Zhong, Bao Shuya, Xi Peng, Yan Ying, Sima Rangju; Sun Wu was also a man of Qi, who later went to Wu.

town:临晋.note: Site of the Wangcheng of the Dali Rong; taken by Qin in 461 BC.

town:五鹿.mod: NE of Puyang, Henan (one view: E of Daming, Hebei)
town:五鹿.note: A Wey town. When Chong'er passed here in exile and begged for food, a peasant gave him a clod of earth; in 632 BC Jin took Wulu.

town:介.note: Jie, a small Eastern Yi state; Ge Lu of Jie once paid court to Lu (631 BC).

town:令支.note: One of the Mountain Rong peoples. In 663 BC Duke Huan of Qi attacked the Mountain Rong in the north, "cutting down Lingzhi and beheading Guzhu".

town:任.note: The small Feng-surnamed state of Ren, by tradition descended from Taihao.

town:共.note: Former state of Gong. After his defeat Gongshu Duan fled to Gong; it later passed to Wey.

town:冀.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Ji; Jin destroyed it and enfeoffed Xi Rui (Ji Rui) there.

town:匡.note: A Wey town. In 496 BC Confucius passed through Kuang, and the people of Kuang, mistaking him for Yang Hu, held him for five days ("the Master was in peril in Kuang").

town:卞.note: A town of the Ji lineage of Lu.

town:卢戎.note: Home of the Lu Rong. In 699 BC Qu Xia of Chu attacked Luo and was defeated by the combined forces of Luo and the Lu Rong.

town:厉.note: The state of Li, a dependency of Chu, later annexed by Chu.

town:句章.note: A Yue town, by tradition built by Goujian.

town:夔.note: The Mi-surnamed state of Kui (a branch fief of Chu), destroyed by Chu in 634 BC for failing to sacrifice to Zhurong and Yuxiong.

town:夷维.note: A town in eastern Qi, home of Yan Ying.

town:姑蔑.note: On Yue's western frontier (Guoyu, "Yue yu": "west to Gumie").

town:孤竹.note: The former state of Boyi and Shuqi; Duke Huan of Qi reached Guzhu in the north during his campaign against the Mountain Rong.

town:寝丘.note: Sunshu Ao's son was enfeoffed here; the land was so poor that no one fought over it, and the family kept it for a long time.

town:屯留.mod: S of Tunliu District, Changzhi, Shanxi
town:屯留.note: Former land of the Liuxu of the Red Di, destroyed by Jin in 593 BC.

town:巩.note: A town within the Zhou royal domain.

town:平阳.note: A Jin town. In 514 BC Jin destroyed the Yangshe lineage and made its land Pingyang County.

town:应.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Ying (enfeoffed to a son of King Wu), absorbed by Chu in the Spring and Autumn; the Ying cemetery is at Pingdingshan.

town:弦.note: The small Kui-surnamed state of Xian, destroyed by Chu in 655 BC.

town:御儿.note: Yue's northern frontier ("north to Yu'er"), bordering Wu.

town:成.note: Former land of the ancient state of Cheng and private town of the Mengsun lineage. In 498 BC, when the three cities were razed, Gonglian Chufu resisted, and Cheng was not razed.

town:房.note: Former land of the state of Fang, destroyed by Chu.

town:无棣.mod: Wudi, Shandong (one view: S of Yanshan, Hebei)
town:无棣.note: Guan Zhong said Qi reached "north to Wudi".

town:无终.note: Wuzhong, a state of the Mountain Rong. In 569 BC Jiafu, viscount of Wuzhong, sent an envoy to Jin, and Wei Jiang urged "peace with the Rong".

town:杜.note: In 687 BC Duke Wu of Qin made Du and Zheng counties.

town:杨.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Yang; Jin destroyed it and gave it to the Yangshe lineage (Shuxiang). In 514 BC the Yangshe lands were divided into three counties.

town:枳.note: A Ba town; many of the tombs of the former kings of Ba were at Zhi (Huayang guozhi).

town:柏.note: Former land of the state of Bai, destroyed by Chu.

town:柏人.note: A Jin town; in 490 BC Zhao Yang besieged the Fan and Zhonghang lineages at Bairen.

town:桐.note: The Yan-surnamed state of Tong, a dependency of Chu. In 508 BC Tong revolted against Chu; Wu had the Shujiu lure the Chu army out and defeated it at Yuzhang.

town:梗阳.note: A Jin town; one of the seven counties created in 514 BC from the lands of the Qi lineage.

town:武城.note: A Lu town. When Ziyou was steward of Wucheng, Confucius heard the sound of strings and singing there.

town:氾.note: A Zheng town. In 636 BC King Xiang of Zhou, fleeing the rebellion of Prince Dai, went out to live at Fan.

town:泺.note: Qi land. In 694 BC Duke Huan of Lu met Duke Xiang of Qi at Luo and was soon murdered in Qi.

town:涂水.note: One of the seven counties created in 514 BC from the lands of the Qi lineage.

town:焦.note: Jiao, a small Ji-surnamed state annexed by Jin; later a key Jin town beyond the He.

town:牟.mod: E of Laiwu District, Jinan, Shandong
town:牟.note: The small state of Mou, a dependency of Lu.

town:王官.note: In 624 BC Duke Mu of Qin crossed the He, burned his boats and took Wangguan and Jiao from Jin, to avenge the Battle of Xiao.

town:番.note: A Chu town; taken by Wu in 504 BC.

town:皋落.note: Home of the Dongshan Gaoluo lineage of the Red Di; attacked by Crown Prince Shensheng of Jin in 660 BC.

town:皖.note: The Yan-surnamed state of Wan (one of the Qunshu group), later part of Chu.

town:祁.note: Fief of Qi Xi, who recommended men of worth without regard to kinship or enmity. In 514 BC Jin destroyed the Qi lineage and divided its lands into seven counties.

town:稷.note: In 594 BC Duke Jing of Jin reviewed his troops at Ji to take over the Di lands.

town:管.note: The state of Guan Shu in the early Zhou; Zheng land in the Spring and Autumn.

town:罗.note: The state of Luo was originally west of Yicheng; Chu annexed it and moved its people here.

town:聊.note: On Qi's western frontier, paired with She in the phrase "east of Liao and She".

town:苦.note: Chen land; by tradition Laozi came from Quren Hamlet, Li Township, Ku County.

town:解.note: A Jin town (Xieliang). Before taking power, Duke Hui of Jin (Yiwu) promised Qin five walled towns beyond the He, "east to the bounds of Guo, south to Mount Hua, and inward as far as the city of Xieliang"; he later broke his word, which led to the Battle of Hanyuan (645 BC).

town:诸暨.note: One of the early capitals of Yue (one view); by tradition Xi Shi came from Mount Zhuluo.

town:谷.note: The Ying-surnamed state of Gu, later part of Chu.

town:豳.note: Where Gong Liu, an ancestral lord of the Zhou, lived; Qin land in the Spring and Autumn.

town:贾.note: The Ji-surnamed state of Jia; Jin destroyed it and enfeoffed Hu Yegu (Jia Ji) there.

town:道.note: Former land of the state of Dao, destroyed by Chu.

town:那处.note: A Chu town. After destroying Quan, King Wu of Chu moved the people of Quan to Nachu.

town:邬.note: One of the seven counties created in 514 BC from the lands of the Qi lineage.

town:邺.note: By tradition Duke Huan of Qi first built the walls of Ye, to shield the Xia states (Guanzi).

town:郇.note: Former land of the Ji-surnamed state of Xun ("the land of Xun and Xia"), later part of Jin.

town:郏.note: A Zheng town. In 541 BC Chu walled Jia as a forward post for its advance north.

town:郑县.note: By tradition where Duke Huan of Zheng was first enfeoffed (one view); later part of Qin, which made it a county in 687 BC.

town:郧.note: The state of Yun, destroyed by Chu (date unknown). In 528 BC King Ping of Chu made Dou Xin lord of Yun; in 506 BC King Zhao of Chu fled to Yun.

town:鄂.note: By tradition Xiong Qu of Chu made his middle son Hong king of E; in the Spring and Autumn a key town on Chu's eastern frontier.

town:鄅.note: The small Yun-surnamed state of Yu. In 524 BC Zhu raided Yu and carried off all its people.

town:酅.note: Ji Ji, the cadet of the house of Ji, took Xi over to Qi (691 BC); Ji split apart and fell the next year.

town:酸枣.note: The former land of the Ji-surnamed state of Southern Yan lay nearby.

town:长葛.note: A Zheng town; taken by Song in 717 BC.

town:阳城.note: By tradition Yu the Great had his capital at Yangcheng; in the Spring and Autumn a town between Zheng and Zhou.

town:阳樊.note: In 635 BC King Xiang of Zhou gave Yangfan to Jin; Cang Ge, a man of Fan, refused to submit, and Duke Wen of Jin "let its people leave".

town:陈仓.note: Duke Wen of Qin obtained the "Treasure of Chen" here and set up a shrine to sacrifice to it.

town:雩娄.mod: E of Shangcheng, Henan (one view: SE of Gushi)
town:雩娄.note: On Chu's eastern frontier, where Wu and Chu fought.

town:项.note: The small state of Xiang, destroyed by Lu in 643 BC (one view: by Qi).

town:须句.note: A small Feng-surnamed state. In 639 BC Zhu destroyed Xuqu, and Duke Xi of Lu attacked Zhu and restored it (his mother Cheng Feng came from Xuqu).

town:颛臾.note: A small Feng-surnamed state, a dependency of Lu: "the Ji lineage is about to attack Zhuanyu", which Confucius condemned (Analects, "Ji Shi").

town:鱼.note: A town of Yong (Yufu). In 611 BC, when Chu attacked Yong, the men of Pi, Shu and Yu pursued the Chu army.

town:鸠兹.note: A Wu town. In 570 BC Zizhong of Chu attacked Wu and took Jiuzi.

town:麇.note: The state of Jun (Xixue). In 611 BC the men of Jun led the Hundred Pu in revolt against Chu.

town:黎.note: The state of the marquis of Li, once driven out by the Red Di; in 594 BC, after destroying the Lu lineage, Jin "set up the marquis of Li and went home".

wall:楚方城.note: A defensive line on Chu's northern frontier, linking forts along the spurs of the Funiu Mountains. In 656 BC Qu Wan told Duke Huan of Qi: "Chu has Fangcheng for its wall and the Han River for its moat." It is seen as a forerunner of the long walls.

wall:齐长城.mod: Pingyin – Mount Tai – Mount Yi – Huangdao, Qingdao, Shandong
wall:齐长城.note: Qi's long wall on its southern border. In the Battle of Pingyin of 555 BC Qi "dug a trench at Fangmen and held it, a li wide"; most scholars take this as the start of the Qi Long Wall, which was then extended east to the sea in stages (course schematic).
